In such a case, Bin Buffering has very large bins (8 times larger than Ola) which might be undesirable: the approximation power of Bin Buffering for range sums is at least 4 times lower than Ola because of the much larger bins. We have seen that Ola can have a competitive advantage when we are interested in getting approximate queries out of the memory buffer. Indeed, Ola supports a wide range of query types using a single memory buffer and relatively small bins. However, as with wavelet-based techniques {{cite:eec9aa0d3a7284dafe8f059a5fcc254c97061dbf}}, {{cite:0e2af1852f6c0f4c010a8d8fe165de4bc4088031}}, {{cite:02b263ec99a74822343d0ff348f8ccb053b6be31}}, Ola can support incrementally better estimates. With wavelet-based methods, one gets approximations by selecting the most significant wavelet coefficients. However, this approach calls for storing all coefficients in order to quickly answer queries within a user-specified error bound. This would be unacceptable for many applications: the wavelet buffer is as large as the external array itself. Incrementally better Ola approximations can be computed by first using the internal buffer, and then adding bins one by one. Indeed, for a given range query, the Ola algorithms involve many bins at both ends of the range. However, only the first few bins have a significant contribution. Recall subsection REF , in which we showed that {{formula:4e3469fc-ae98-4616-be7c-48545f11651f}} was given by {{formula:0d2f610f-f0c7-4b70-ae01-94a0c57431e8}} where {{formula:31fbd5f9-8e41-4642-bd9b-611a79919535}} is a Lagrange interpolation of the range query function {{formula:8a74838f-a0c1-416a-85d3-1178337efb8c}} . Only when the function {{formula:7e071825-878a-4305-8fb9-1313562be225}} goes from a polynomial to 0 is there a difference between the target range function {{formula:277e903e-7435-4e9b-a584-4663c5e28eb5}} and the range function {{formula:9b6d4df6-5202-4604-a583-bbe97d92aff6}} estimated by bin-wise Lagrange interpolation. However, the error made by Lagrange interpolation also diminishes as we move away from the bin containing the edge of the range. In many cases, it might be sufficient to take into account only 1 or 3 bins near the edge (at each endpoint of the range). For example, consider {{formula:b74f6063-a713-47fe-bf7f-27e63d19f785}} , {{formula:ae43c79d-d662-4b5c-b0e2-d28cf68bbc90}} with {{formula:3cc03909-f490-45c9-a37d-29c5b0262d27}} for {{formula:a4338820-e095-4a78-96c7-c98eda7b001b}} and 0 otherwise. A numerical evaluation shows that using only one bin at each endpoint instead of the required 3 will take care of 86% of the error when range edges are in the middle of a bin. The result is more significant for larger {{formula:651498a8-2b23-4167-bdd3-6124c24aa343}} , for example, for {{formula:e87c9754-eff6-41a4-bebe-439de91f1962}} , we need 15 bins at each endpoint for a complete evaluation; however, if we use only 5 centered, we take care of 97% of the error. (See Figure REF .) In short, Ola can provide wavelet-like progressive evaluation of the queries simply by querying fewer bins in the external array. We can analyze more mathematically the relationship between the number of bins used at each end of the range and the error. First note that bin-wise Lagrange interpolation is linear: if we interpolate the sequence {{formula:a595a895-45b1-4c14-801a-0db5ad47d95d}} and the sequence {{formula:77ce7320-2754-4c40-9de2-7e37ff91782f}} , then the sum of the two interpolants is just the interpolation of the sequence {{formula:6ed157bf-3dcd-412e-97cb-516f74a2bbca}} . Hence, it is sufficient to consider only one non-zero sample value at any given time. We proceed to show that the contribution of a sample value {{formula:7bab7378-a16c-49db-9ffa-ddd329ac460b}} to bin-wise Lagrange interpolation decays quickly past one bin. Let {{formula:2373713a-d9b1-4776-97a3-11285e704a41}} be fixed, and consider the interpolation of the sequence {{formula:c512770e-0f61-4486-b2e7-8e3029f88160}} , {{formula:bb06163d-a9a0-4a0e-98db-deab02ba0e20}} for all {{formula:52f499c9-31f6-4ef4-9e99-d6fc927a0544}} . We can then consider the interpolant {{formula:e5a8e810-833d-4a94-8a2b-8edb61eafa2d}} in the {{formula:71766955-dbe4-422c-b117-e778c595a0cf}} bin defined by the interval {{formula:0dbe5af3-95c1-4e91-a457-934489ecb359}} . Clearly the denominator will increase sharply in absolute value as {{formula:9b2989d5-574f-41a7-9f6e-2e29e8428a4b}} grows. We show that the numerator is non increasing in {{formula:4d16133f-43dd-4e70-932a-1a5d554a1373}} . Setting {{formula:f9199149-d4a3-4579-b663-87d4f9227445}} , we have {{formula:4fac8d27-568f-4156-9b73-4141a4793133}} . On the other hand, the denominator in absolute value, {{formula:29ad62ce-e8d8-49bd-9776-2aa3272c37ab}} . Setting {{formula:3f63425d-076c-4f29-af28-7a06f72815d0}} , we have {{formula:f63f921d-e7d6-4fb4-9a56-0c5e229b99be}} which has a rate of increase of starting at {{formula:56add60e-a32f-4208-96be-c3debcd91320}} and rising with {{formula:21b2de06-083b-4c66-8223-0cd267d013d9}} . Hence, the amplitude of the polynomial decreases faster than exponentially as {{formula:a50cea20-2bc3-4245-be99-2d131b971936}} increases. It is difficult to compare the progressive approximation we get using this approach with related wavelet-based ones. Wavelet-based algorithms do not use the original array as a data source when answering queries and thus, they have much larger storage requirements. For large-scale applications, approximate queries are required for wavelet-based algorithms because storing all the coefficients is unthinkable whereas Ola has progressive approximate queries as an added option. {{figure:09d86f14-1aa1-417a-a5ee-5e25640eb88c}} This paper has considered bin-buffering algorithms and showed that using a hierarchical approach, highly scalable algebraic queries were possible even with a small buffer. Using overlapped bins, we have shown that we could buffer several local moments simultaneously and use much less storage than wavelet-based approaches while still supporting progressive queries and very scalable queries and updates. In short, we showed that {{formula:beb28896-8869-4852-86b6-6634bb8f6571}} local moments could be buffered using only a single real-valued buffer: using bins of a fixed size irrespective of {{formula:da296d68-b55a-4f67-89d0-27f235a52e9c}} . Other types of range queries could also be grouped and buffered efficiently together {{cite:3ef5da4a02bb793893168133bd5a62bb433cc576}}. By a direct product {{cite:aa49b595a8cf654ccc092582befe47263fd8efa8}}, Hierarchical Bin Buffering and therefore the Ola approach can be generalized to the multidimensional case. Some implementation issues were not addressed. For example, many forms of buffering using finite-accuracy floating-point numbers are susceptible to significant numerical errors. Finally, the source code used for the production of this paper is freely available {{cite:cdac3b577396445090fa52fc9f277b0d703ee418}}.

section_text: limitations: the communication graph is often assumed to be complete (or all-to-all), but in the absence of communication, the time-evolution of the systems' variables can be oscillatory or even chaotic. The system dynamics can be modified through the information exchange, and, as in the consensus problem, the goal of the interconnection is to reach synchronization to a common solution of the individual dynamics {{cite:8e3157379ef855482fcaf37fe9405ef51457a194}}, {{cite:684dc66e7d4a0631af50bd0baaeacb3bded11a07}}, {{cite:f2645858041eedb262e8cf7c96110637549c6792}}, {{cite:a21a35419d06741d5fa243f5c23f57f052b23620}}. Coordination problems encountered in the engineering world can often be rephrased as consensus or synchronization problems in which both the individual dynamics and the limited communication aspects play an important role. Designing interconnection control laws that can ensure synchronization of relevant variables is therefore a control problem that has attracted quite some attention in the recent years {{cite:3377176d8288814ff87c2dcfec20886d46780b65}}, {{cite:eb37f7114d6e7372c9c8d3c28bb100b08549eba5}}, {{cite:ae1621740a416c2873da35e86d33235d86024dc4}}, {{cite:032e7777248339fbdefded6f736f9ef54ceaf1f0}}, {{cite:fddc190ba04b15335e89d3e7f9f53df5b14d3eec}}. The present paper deals with a fairly general solution of the synchronization problem in the linear case. Assuming {{formula:736e8374-8f6f-4274-9cc6-d310fe71f3fa}} identical individual agents dynamics each described by the linear state-space model {{formula:2e1c1824-d387-447b-98b6-5f6625e21191}} , the main result is the construction of a dynamic output feedback controller that ensures exponential synchronization to a solution of the linear system {{formula:11890e3c-ed7f-4568-907c-9bbb4a824b68}} under the following assumptions: (i) {{formula:7a4cf05b-7fe9-4241-bd9f-c1b2f0d07340}} has no exponentially unstable mode, (ii) {{formula:69adb29b-ffa1-4408-889e-ae47c6506ba6}} is stabilizable and {{formula:7ada616a-9eb7-4725-9f61-896962265488}} is detectable, and (iii) the communication graph is uniformly connected. The result can be interpreted as a generalization of classical consensus algorithms, studied recently, corresponding to the particular case {{formula:b2c34407-09b6-4eb9-8873-58057cc5291b}} {{cite:0611b2b233fdc26e63788eca79cf783b27bc1c4b}}, {{cite:dffa2ea9c3c6665ef5522c572c54d2f0cecb647c}}. The generalization includes the non-trivial examples of synchronizing harmonic oscillators or chains of integrators. The proposed dynamic controller structure proposed in this paper differs from the static diffusive coupling often considered in the synchronization literature, which requires more stringent assumptions on the communication graph. For instance, the results in the recent paper {{cite:c1e1ffa3ebab1a8473177d4fd4cce2b7b0e7b4ff}} assume a time-invariant topology. The paper also provides sufficient conditions for synchronization by static diffusive coupling and illustrates on simple examples that synchronization may fail under diffusive coupling when the stronger assumptions on the communication graph are not satisfied. The paper is organized as follows. In Section the notation used throughout the paper is summarized, some preliminary results are reviewed and the synchronization problem is introduced and defined. In Section the linear case is studied when state coupling among the systems is allowed while in Section the output coupling case is considered. In Section we extend the main results to discrete-time linear systems and to periodic time-varying linear systems. Finally, in Section , two-dimensional examples are reported to illustrate the role of the proposed dynamic controller in situations where static diffusive coupling fails to achieve synchronization. section_text: Future work that studies this method with the inclusion of humans that help to validate and “clean" the recommended metadata would be telling of how much this method is able to speed up the process of generating accurate and reliable metadata for metadata-poor resources. Such an analysis is left to future research. Finally, multiplicative effects due to particle interaction may effect the results of the algorithm. For instance, if two particles, {{formula:259b42d2-baa5-450b-b757-10dec3ad9808}} and {{formula:6bc0533a-75fe-4e38-811f-39afda2f9096}} , meet at a particular node, {{formula:ce269697-9b00-45cc-853f-a1ecda243696}} , and {{formula:b85f1c22-1d44-44b3-ae8c-cc1e2f6946f8}} and {{formula:ad79b342-7582-4f30-9ed8-c6bf27d05b3a}} have similar metadata then the footprint they leave at {{formula:eabf6d95-a9d8-4b7e-a89b-774502603579}} should be more noticeable. Because two different metadata sources are supplying the same property values, there is an increased probability of that recommended metadata value being correct. Currently, only a summation is being provided. It may be interesting to multiply this summation by the number of unique particles that provided energy for a particular recommended metadata value. The variations of this preliminary framework will be explored in future work. Automatic metadata generation is becoming an increasingly important field of research as digital library repositories become more prevalent and move into the arena of less strongly controlled, decentralized collections (e.g. arXiv and CiteSeer). The creation and maintenance of high-quality, detailed metadata is hampered on numerous levels. Manual metadata creation methods are costly. Recent efforts to leverage the collective power of social tagging (i.e. “folksonomies") may address some of the shortcomings of the manual creation of metadata and result in viable models for online resources that do not require strongly controlled vocabularies and metadata ontologies. However, it is doubtful that “folksonomies" can be generalized to situations that require vetted, well-standardized metadata. The automated creation of metadata on the basis of content-analysis is a promising alternative to the manual creation of metadata. It is conceivably more efficient in situations where textual data is available and allows for more formal control of the type and nature of metadata that is extracted. However, it can be unreliable for non-text resources, yield low-quality metadata and can be computationally expensive. This article proposed another possible component of the metadata generation toolkit which may complement and support the above mentioned approaches. Instead of creating new metadata, metadata is propagated from a metadata-rich subset of the collection to similar, but metadata-poor subsets. The substrate for this extrapolation is an associative network of resource relations created from other available metadata. Metadata propagation may provide a computationally feasible means of generating large amounts of metadata for heterogeneous resources which can later be fine-tuned by manual intervention or cross-validation with content-based methods. The article finally provided experimental results using the High-Energy Physics bibliographic data set (hep-th 2003). Human intervention may play an important role in fine-tuning the metadata propagation algorithm. The results of this experiment are promising and there still exists a range of potential modifications to this basic framework that may lead to even better results. This research was financially supported by the Research Library at the Los Alamos National Laboratory. The modified hep-th 2003 bibliographic dataset was generously provided by Shou-de Lin and Jennifer H. Watkins provided editorial assistance. Finally, the hep-th 2003 database is based on data from the arXiv archive and the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center SPIRES-HEP database provided for the 2003 KDD Cup competition with additional preparation performed by the Knowledge Discovery Laboratory, University of Massachusetts Amherst.

section_text: open problems in S:openproblems, and conclude in S:conc. In this section we outline the physics that naturally leads us to consider Hankel hollow weighing matrices. For a more detailed discussion of the physics, see {{cite:4efe9dd016c2d263d418ae82099bd3cb8553ffa5}}, {{cite:56dc7cfcdebe51a8579d1e2db4a3600c1194d8fc}}, {{cite:3dd411ffa58524ec957504450bf4b0ff7688bc5d}}, {{cite:d056802759dcadf80d8c2aabd03c3bbbca179c4e}}. The resonant frequencies of an optical cavity are defined classically as the modes which constructively interfere inside the cavity. Because they are evenly spaced, they form a so-called a frequency comb. By placing a nonlinear medium inside the cavity, pump photons with frequency {{formula:06b8e4e9-9b60-4670-b38c-e6013b9642d0}} can downconvert into an entangled pair of photons, so long as the new photons' frequencies satisfy an energy conservation constraint, {{formula:61cb8668-cc6b-4cf4-af1c-cf318a8d881b}} where {{formula:8b83cce0-ff5e-48e7-9065-5462f97f3907}} and {{formula:4755ab92-e065-4513-a956-6907db8209d5}} are the {{formula:79e084d4-6c58-4a3d-b2a1-bf3b3d81c0ab}} and {{formula:db9c4c31-a13b-4e00-8f19-f4768563d908}} resonant frequencies of the cavity. The range over which the downconversion can occur is limited by the phasematching bandwidth of the cavity. More generally, multiple frequencies can be simultaneously phasematched inside the cavity, and upconversion is allowed as well as downconversion. The total Hamiltonian is then idealized by the following {{formula:5b7ef421-5039-436f-a14a-14c9017e8c47}} where {{formula:579ff936-9bd1-4d48-9076-5d75f051ab3a}} is the (discrete) spectrum of the polychromatic pump, {{formula:850f0442-2a18-4eb0-85a9-3d049fbf2f5c}} is a global coupling strength, {{formula:6e13caad-5aa3-47c8-9685-77681e87ddb9}} is the creation operator for the {{formula:a774e812-555e-401c-b889-ef3e2a7fa628}} mode, and {{formula:1e50ab33-0ad0-4070-a102-ead940c0bfd5}} are matrix elements of a symmetric matrix. In units of the fundamental frequency of the cavity, the restriction of the inner sum to terms with {{formula:a6bf9071-4f13-44fa-99e2-79c4339b860a}} enforces photon energy conservation, and the magnitude of {{formula:57922dd0-52d9-4d9e-896c-1a1b4f8f55ae}} determines the strength of the coupling in units of {{formula:d7ddafd8-7e1e-42d6-961d-7ba436849013}} , while the sign determines whether the photons are upconverted or downconverted. If all of the coupling strengths are equal, then {{formula:cc3e5396-b738-46c9-b2b0-cacd97d6e9cd}} is a Hankel matrix whose elements are either 0 or {{formula:467fe22b-4118-4b45-bd52-6adc950dc5a3}} , where {{formula:8dd1188d-07a4-4162-85e9-a12693c4f3e2}} is a constant. Experimental simplicity further demands that there is no single-mode squeezing and hence we require that the elements along the main diagonal of {{formula:43027b33-de55-40d9-9ce9-8f9bbb8f22d8}} are all zero, i.e. {{formula:0ff48cf1-93f4-4b22-9ba6-2c86a44040fb}} must be a hollow matrix. The Hamiltonian E:Hamiltonian can be used to create continuous-variable cluster states, defined as Gaussian states satisfying the relation {{formula:c13a3c0b-1ab6-4f74-bad5-d7cb72357953}} where {{formula:37d972ae-2e57-4866-aed6-7da7045feb17}} and {{formula:917705ef-a52f-4b7d-8b60-73ebc739d3e5}} are vectors of amplitude and phase quadratures for the {{formula:f69e45bd-899f-42d6-9514-dda2f7997639}} cavity mode, {{formula:b7e89264-299a-4bac-b7aa-890e2d13e9a0}} and {{formula:76a6c5ab-9706-4a3b-a52a-43a12cfaf220}} , {{formula:d0fc3f01-64d9-45a1-b76d-b4c7bb24c10e}} is the symmetric weighted adjacency matrix of the graph of the CVCS, and the arrow denotes the limit of large squeezing. Reference {{cite:56dc7cfcdebe51a8579d1e2db4a3600c1194d8fc}} first proved a nonunique relationship between the adjacency matrix {{formula:65254acd-a00f-40a7-9c56-ff1118aee2ee}} , which describes the cluster state, and the adjacency matrix {{formula:2be4014c-0566-4c10-b14e-5dacd5b33cfb}} , which describes the coupling between the modes inside the cavity. The general relationship is somewhat complicated, so references {{cite:3dd411ffa58524ec957504450bf4b0ff7688bc5d}}, {{cite:4efe9dd016c2d263d418ae82099bd3cb8553ffa5}}, {{cite:d056802759dcadf80d8c2aabd03c3bbbca179c4e}} introduced the simplifying ansatz that {{formula:97d162fe-0b8e-41b4-97b6-f1a9bb98d66a}} from which it follows {{cite:3dd411ffa58524ec957504450bf4b0ff7688bc5d}}, {{cite:d056802759dcadf80d8c2aabd03c3bbbca179c4e}} that (up to a trivial relabeling) {{formula:c22842cb-b6de-44f0-9fe3-4f90128bee15}} In short, assuming {{formula:d9219d87-704c-4b1a-87a4-66c929b39fa9}} is an orthogonal matrix implies the graph describing the couplings between photons in the cavity ({{formula:afc3fa8e-4297-4a36-8182-0345fd262ce3}} ) is identical to the graph describing the cluster state ({{formula:2b30f2fc-18b9-45f3-8dd8-a55947fd8bd3}} ), which is a vast simplification over the general relationship. The derivation requires that {{formula:7df42901-2524-4fd2-a9b5-33b8129a0870}} be the adjacency matrix of a bipartite graph, but as we will see, one can derive this from the Hankel and hollow constraints. We now see how the twin demands of experimental and theoretical simplicity for creating CVCS in an optical cavity naturally lead us to consider Hankel hollow orthogonal matrices, all of whose non-zero elements are either {{formula:f56bc9c3-8b2f-4d8d-9fa9-86fb372f95d5}} , for some constant {{formula:cfbe24b8-6a48-48f6-b142-bcae64e00c9f}} . We can of course consider renormalized matrices instead by dividing out {{formula:6f510777-bb3c-4198-831b-c20d958b1363}} , so that all entries are {{formula:2045d900-7805-496c-8ac0-131dc2a6e1c8}} ; after finding these renormalized matrices, we can then reintroduce the constant afterwards so that E:Asquared holds. Thus, we see that finding and classifying Hankel hollow weighing matrices is our primary interest. For completeness, we mention one further elaboration that is possible for this scheme. If the photons' polarization, transverse, or spatial degrees of freedom are taken into account, then the Hamiltonian E:Hamiltonian can be modified by adding additional indices for these modes. If these additional modes are all frequency-degenerate, then an additional sum over these degenerate modes appears in E:Hamiltonian, which allows for the symmetric intercoupling between the degenerate degrees of freedom. If such an interaction could be simultaneously phasematched by the nonlinear medium inside the cavity, then one is naturally lead to consider block-Hankel matrices, where the size of the blocks is equal to the number of degenerate degrees of freedom. We leave the consideration of block-Hankel hollow weighing matrices to future work. In this section we introduce the definition of anticirculant graphs and study some of their first properties. For the sake of self-containedness, we will define here all the graph-theoretic concepts we require. For further background on theory of graphs the interested reader is referred to the book by Diestel {{cite:24838f6f33b693e443cca46373d1dde0692fc3bd}}. Our reference about permutations and finite groups is Cameron {{cite:c4e07fc53a27594c2be294b50923af92574cccf3}}. We will work with simple graphs. A (simple) graph {{formula:4c649e43-0efc-4b81-8e59-7e7f559ea683}} is an ordered pair of sets defined as follows: {{formula:9de57558-cb27-4303-b380-b4e43544c8f8}} is a non-empty set, whose elements are called vertices; {{formula:b30f0d9c-e794-419a-b604-13950e9d87e5}} is a non-empty set of unordered pairs of vertices, whose elements are called edges. An edge of the form {{formula:25dd71ed-6449-47d0-b532-c29ffb934aa3}} is called a loop. Two vertices {{formula:10b5f563-17a8-4b31-ab5a-8adbb3c1d38f}} and {{formula:f971293d-3e5b-4ab1-b716-c42354fbca42}} are said to be adjacent if {{formula:d4f1597e-6e44-45cf-9b04-40ca9747e2d1}} . Often, this is simply denoted by writing {{formula:9625e869-1d8d-4b73-91d7-b2579b755ce5}} . A graph is loopless if it is has no loops. The adjacency matrix of a graph {{formula:d566257e-35f5-4ddc-b733-386808d58b05}} is denoted by {{formula:39665e85-baa4-4a47-8ebe-fbcda9bbb7bf}} and defined by {{formula:02303df8-2fba-4303-a5a7-cad246cd509a}} An adjacency matrix of a loopless graph is said to be hollow. The degree of a vertex {{formula:0b1ba962-4df7-4ff7-9452-2ce42190a263}} in a graph {{formula:0e43c949-8a1e-422e-8d6d-a402b43f2a67}}

section_text: limitations and current (typical) precisions. Table 1 provides a summary of the methods discussed in detail below. {{table:67942bf9-1a5d-4406-b397-f7379833015d}} The most straightforward way to age-date an individual brown dwarf is to borrow from its environment, a tactic that is suitable for members of coeval clusters/associations and companions to age-dated stars. Brown dwarfs are well-sampled down to and below the deuterium fusing mass limit (M {{formula:c8a349ce-636d-43f4-bab2-0cb3319d7cb6}} 0.013 M{{formula:d0fbbffc-95bf-4633-b5e8-9575ac78911e}} ) in the youngest nearby clusters ({{formula:948f7e90-0ecc-489d-8b26-ecbb263678db}} {{formula:8c2f00e5-7217-4422-877c-a1eb14475eda}} 5 Myr), as their luminosities are greater at early ages. Brown dwarfs have also been identified in somewhat older (10–50 Myr)“loose associations” in the vicinity of the Sun ({{formula:9cfa10b6-30cb-4031-897f-5c96275e3bde}} {{formula:9cbdbdfb-ef9b-4aea-befe-84be9eb2f8c5}} 50–100 pc; e.g., {{cite:15f44987c00c2b2c90a1607b6160c901c1aec91a}}). For older and more distant clusters ({{formula:83b41c4b-48c1-487a-a353-8178d9b31b89}} {{formula:690b614b-3bd5-4319-b3ff-87fa70b66e4b}} 1 kpc), decreasing surface temperatures and compact radii exacerbate the sensitivity issues that plague low-mass stellar studies (see contribution by G. Piotto). There are as yet no known brown dwarfs in globular clusters, despite detection of the end of the stellar main sequence in systems such as NGC 6397 {{cite:c3aec005bae16b8b016b152ed6e95e913ebbba61}}. For brown dwarfs in young clusters, numerous studies have examined age-related trends in colors (e.g., {{cite:ed91b8da3b41f6438d06892edbbf3ee46a47aada}}), spectral characteristics (e.g., {{cite:6d02497190066bfb3e6db4becc621e12240d8bfe}}), accretion timescales (e.g., {{cite:5824d928b0c3153c36288041e9f25861d4c851ec}}) and circum(sub)stellar disk evolution (e.g., {{cite:06ee4a9220fefb3f0be20346894f41b1319014a5}}). These have been coarsely quantified, and appear to be most useful at very young ages ({{formula:f6f71487-1f38-401e-93b1-b41140900d04}} 10 Myr). Surface properties and luminosities are highly variable at these ages due to sensitivity to formation conditions (e.g., {{cite:c5cc0a11710490811486e6b9d14804e54b1b53bd}}), ongoing accretion, complex magnetic effects (e.g., {{cite:fc93e941df80ffc048a92610918a627d5cad904c}}) and age spreads within a cluster (see contribution by R. Jeffries). Hence, while brown dwarfs in clusters with ages spanning {{formula:d04cab8f-1ad5-4f29-8829-12127be65e27}} 1–650 Myr are now well-documented, with age uncertainties as good as 10% (for the LDB technique; see {{formula:2752efcf-bf12-4728-b9ad-906588d5f8b6}} 3), useful predictive trends are probably limited to ages of {{formula:0e4883ac-4a31-445b-9a11-524283ca5db6}} 10 Myr. Known brown dwarf companions to main sequence stars now number a few dozen, spanning a wide range of separation, age and composition. Many of these systems are widely-separated so that their brown dwarf companions can be directly studied. Age uncertainties for companion brown dwarfs depend on stellar dating methods which are generally more uncertain (50–100%; e.g., {{cite:2846bd411a46d3033c7ace28d4b8d255ace1785e}}) than cluster ages. Searches for substellar companions to more precisely age-dated white dwarfs (e.g. {{cite:83e6d0a5494a6f0fdbad6697a9c46cf831bf1a6a}}, {{cite:c27d7df5faca8aba6723804766afa5a4e49bba75}}) and subgiants {{cite:b8139efc3091db6b2604210afb1c5ed65573ba4f}} have so far met with limited success. Nevertheless, brown dwarf companions to age-dated stars serve as important benchmarks for calibrating other age-dating methods at late ages ({{formula:c75a3202-9e01-42fa-92f1-9c09a435267b}} 500 Myr) and are fundamental for testing evolutionary models (see contribution by T. Dupuy). Lithium is fused at a lower temperature than hydrogen (2.5{{formula:cf67f965-09e2-493d-b267-4b03c1ec73e8}} 10{{formula:891d6978-1c0c-4d95-921f-01f3ef3a86f9}} K), resulting in a somewhat lower fusing mass limit (0.065 M{{formula:dbed2bf3-07ce-4e0b-a1e9-b6f2b17b6542}} ; {{cite:e56827c6774e756dc66db9a31d4182ddfe03b275}}). Because the interiors of low mass stars and brown dwarfs are fully convective at early ages, an object with a mass above this limit will fully deplete its initial reservoir of lithium within {{formula:1e5696d9-60b2-4638-a668-65e4af396991}} 200 Myr. Hence, any system older than this which exhibits Li I absorption has a mass less than 0.065 M{{formula:0be468ff-5122-4aa7-93dc-3031536f4187}} and is therefore a brown dwarf (e.g., {{cite:0c902710e5720aec64c89f9b33a6ff410227a8fb}}). With a mass limit, one can use evolutionary models to determine an age limit. In the age range {{formula:b02712a0-f638-44bc-a613-fab77a625628}} 10–200 Myr, the degree of lithium depletion in low-mass stars and brown dwarfs is itself mass-dependent, occurring earlier in more massive stars which first achieve the necessary core temperatures. Hence, over this range the age of an individual source can be precisely constrained if its mass is known. A more practical approach, however, is to ascertain the age of a group of coeval low-mass objects based on which sources do or do not exhibit Li I absorption; this is the lithium depletion boundary (LDB) technique. Different evolutionary models yield remarkably similar predictions for the location of the LDB over a broad range of ages {{cite:941cd1870230b9e4d007f12acad1b516f7fd9d17}}, and the boundary itself is readily identifiable in color-magnitude diagrams. As such, this technique has been used to age-date several nearby young clusters and associations (e.g., {{cite:5f4c473f4a626eb7b813da038e19762f25362cdb}}, {{cite:0aa86035ed3570d1faf6a667580310e96f3752cd}}, {{cite:a539d773f3285dc40c56bb63d2d2755c693ea5b3}}, {{cite:d0ed153c67c33b36fcac16e67b9643f6e70c7998}}). LDB studies have also provided independent confirmation of other cluster-dating methods such as isochrone fitting {{cite:a539d773f3285dc40c56bb63d2d2755c693ea5b3}}. A variant of the LDB technique for coeval binary systems has been proposed by {{cite:17984f83a2310cd48d75b477084a8897b2300087}}, in which a system that exhibits Li I absorption in the secondary but not in the primary can have both lower and upper age limits assigned to it (note that the presence/absence of Li I in both components simply sets a single upper/lower age limit). This technique requires resolved optical spectroscopy of both components and can be pursued only for a few (rare) wide low-mass pairs (e.g., Burgasser et al., in prep.) or using high spatial-resolution spectroscopy (e.g. {{cite:09db6dfd8019c882d6da74c45a9487139c06e08b}}). No single brown dwarf pair straddling the LDB has yet been identified. Despite its utility, the detection of LI I absorption in brown dwarf spectra has limitations. The 6708 Å line lies in an relatively faint spectral region for cool L-type dwarfs, so sensitive spectral observations on large telescopes are typically required to detect (or convincingly rule out) this feature. For optically-brighter M-type brown dwarfs, high-resolution observations are generally required to distinguish Li I absorption from overlapping molecular absorption features. Young brown dwarfs ({{formula:87369e06-cec4-46cc-8511-286c1e16ef36}} 50 Myr) with low surface gravities show weakened alkali line absorption (see {{formula:df33d6ef-3020-4acf-809e-f839464296be}} 5), including Li I, making it again necessary to obtain sensitive, high-resolution observations {{cite:15f44987c00c2b2c90a1607b6160c901c1aec91a}}. For brown dwarfs cooler than {{formula:e0c2aa9c-6148-4794-8b6d-b3243dc501a3}} 1500 K (i.e., the T dwarfs), lithium is chemically depleted in the photosphere through its conversion to LiCl, LiF or LiOH {{cite:58bb262fbbae7790bd0028d0996a7cd72afdc9fb}}. section_text: future work is to implement the extension of {{formula:ad15ca6c-738b-4891-ada8-7ac72601065b}} by such user friendly path expressions like in the following example queryThe keyword path is added to aid reading. (for simplicity only involving set constants for full set names from the bibliographic WDB): set query separate { pub-type:x in BibDB where exists path <b1>refers-to*<x>refers-to<b2> . 'author':"Smith" in x }; The result of this query would be: Result = { paper:p2 } Quantification goes over paths from b1 to b2 having an appropriate intermediate set (or node for a publication) x which is required to have the element author:"Smith", but it appears that there does not exists such an explicit path. Nevertheless, the required path does exist, as shown in Figure REF by the dashed edges labelled refers-to leading from b1 to p3, where p3 is equal (bisimilar) to b2 (p3{{formula:c5e7efad-c1ca-4b24-b2a4-0e8301de8b46}}b2) as we already know. In strongly extensional graphs (where there are no bisimilar nodes) path expressions would be understood quite straightforwardly. Our hyperset approach leads to such kind of complications, but this is the compromise for having a natural language with clear semantics and strong (also precisely characterised) expressive power. Note that the result of the above query would be the empty set if the Kleene star “*” was removed from the path expression. Indeed, there are no paths of length two from b1 to b2, even up to bisimulation. {{figure:c973ecb9-c8ab-4ac9-b359-574529a2fb0a}} The action of the path expression <b1>refers-to*<x>refers-to<b2> can, in fact, be “rewritten” into {{formula:6eb8b891-e9fd-4574-af3f-07f6e3f87f53}} (in its present form) by the following steps. Firstly, consider the subexpression <x>refers-to<b2> denoting a path from the candidate publication x to b2 labelled by 'refers-to'. This can be expressed as the {{formula:da4f36ed-07b3-4e16-acac-bee1e19839b6}} -formula: 'refers-to':b2 in x where b2 is set constant and x is set variable. Secondly, the subpath expression <b1>refers-to*<x> denotes set of candidate publications x which can be reached from b1 by navigating zero or more refers-to labelled edges. Thus, let us include in the library the general set query which will give the set of graph nodes (of a graph representing a hyperset z) reachable by navigating zero or more l-labelled edges. set query TC_along_label(label l, set z) be recursion p { k:x in TC(z) where ( ( x=z and k='null' ) or ( k=l and exists m:y in p . l:x in y ) ) }; Here p is a recursion set variable to representing the set T=TC_along_label(l,z) of nodes lying on potentially all the l-labelled paths outgoing from z. All elements of T are l-labelled, except possibly z. If l:z is in z then l:z will be added to T. But in any case 'null':z will appear in T at the first stage of iteration. Hence the query call TC_along_label('refers-to', b1) represents the path expression <b1>refers-to*<x> where 'refers-to' is label value and b1 is set constant. Finally the path expression <b1>refers-to*<x>refers-to<b2>, understood as the set of all x lying on the paths matching this path expression, is expressed as: set query separate { n:xx in call TC_along_label('refers-to', b1) where 'refers-to':b2 in xx }; Now, the fragment exists path <b1>refers-to*<x>refers-to<b2> . 'author':"Smith" in x of our path expression query can be rewritten as exists m:y in separate {n:xx in call TC_along_label('refers-to',b1) where 'refers-to':b2 in xx } . (x=y and 'author':"Smith" in x) so that we can insert it in the full query set query let set constant BibDB = http://www.csc.liv.ac.uk/~molyneux/t/BibDB-f1.xml#BibDB, set constant b1 = http://www.csc.liv.ac.uk/~molyneux/t/BibDB-f1.xml#b1, set constant b2 = http://www.csc.liv.ac.uk/~molyneux/t/BibDB-f1.xml#b2 in separate { pub-type:x in BibDB where exists m:y in separate { n:xx in call TC_along_label('refers-to',b1) where 'refers-to':b2 in xx } . ( x=y and 'author':"Smith" in x) } endlet; and run it to see the required result: Query is well-formed, well-typed and executable Result = { 'paper':http://www.csc.liv.ac.uk/~molyneux/t/BibDB-f2.xml#p2 } Finished in: 5766 ms (query execution is 5764 ms, and postprocessing time is 2 ms) Despite this example of successfully imitating path expressions it would be more useful to also include path expressions directly within the implementation language. Although much more general path expressions can be imitated by {{formula:c568afc9-db5d-43be-ac48-ba389bdb664d}} -queries in the current version {{cite:d66ab022dfe910996640ddb43979b330285256b8}}, this imitation can be quite complicated in general and is not a particularly efficient way of implementing and executing queries with path expressions. Anyway, the {{formula:46bd1e2c-6b5c-43a9-940c-d27bac435127}} -language, as it is implemented now, is very expressive. The query example considered in this section has mainly theoretical interest, although it might be useful in practice. The point is that we can define in {{formula:66b8c1ff-8d5c-4958-8e7e-f33447eab283}} linear ordering on the transitive closure of any hyperset by using the lexicographical linear ordering we have on labels. In fact, the resulting linear ordering on hypersets is itself, in a sense, lexicographical. Having defined linear ordering, we can further define any (“generic” polynomial-time) computable operation over hypersets by simulating any given Turing Machine (as shown in descriptive complexity theory {{cite:747745a982797317a7acab77c21b247540ab832a}}, {{cite:0337bd8ba86be77b2cda3973499f60103cd366fc}}, {{cite:3d342ddc3127521c16a9ddbd403a68793ecbe2e9}}, {{cite:81d25b9dbc9cf66ec1187f6e7a4190c0d0ce30c5}}). This is the key point of the main result in {{cite:40baf6ff4f0f28300a5708c8b547f54f782c8963}} (for well-founded sets) and in {{cite:403f51932f80590405acc86eafd1e080f1573857}}, {{cite:e11d47cf180b2086db327243e644b86ef5dfcb8a}}, {{cite:146c1f0d74b2fe28665a4a064cd91dc3896bf03b}} (for hypersets) on the expressive power of {{formula:828c19ce-8791-419f-8596-4cba33b40874}} coinciding with polynomial time computability over (hyper)sets. (We omit precise formulation which is more subtle in the case of hypersets having labelled elements; see {{cite:40baf6ff4f0f28300a5708c8b547f54f782c8963}}, {{cite:e11d47cf180b2086db327243e644b86ef5dfcb8a}}). section_text: open problems for the reader. Throughout this paper, {{formula:f5757fcb-9f18-4e78-bfc1-d3b0a827ac5b}} will denote a complete, cocomplete category, while {{formula:8cef708b-196d-4b65-9e4c-021343803d8f}} stands for a small category. In general, for notions pertaining to category theory, we refer to {{cite:9a167d9fd4d622832b0843ee9a5656fc06738694}}. The convention for composing morphisms is the usual one: given two morphisms {{formula:a2243cde-c8d5-411a-8e85-446fb6377fc0}} and {{formula:ad2df10e-3caa-4540-8392-b80ee3e6f224}} in a category, their composition is {{formula:8422a6ea-0a07-40cb-8bce-4d975b86d9a1}} . In order to keep the notation simple, if {{formula:09918c8b-3312-4e24-9c70-24e43b2075a9}} is an object of {{formula:bc654868-d96c-4bfa-9eaa-7b8c9c5530fd}} we write {{formula:3cfe6ef4-3d8d-461d-8201-fb9be5dee9eb}} (rather than {{formula:d5e6d26d-dde8-4ec7-b7be-fb2498252658}} , for example). Sometimes, in order to make it easier to keep track of the objects involved in morphisms, we shall denote {{formula:03089ea9-6343-4650-bc58-91e39f44c371}} by {{formula:8554e8ab-9511-4139-940d-86bcd18acfbf}} . Similarly, we might denote a subset {{formula:a5a5d0e8-2907-4ef5-8d46-549184fc970d}} by {{formula:2e6a42a7-4245-4623-b2c3-897f5c056ee0}} . Given a set {{formula:2d7bdbba-c7a5-4bc5-9c8b-fc4ec0e20f80}} and a morphism {{formula:42c58e55-c170-43b3-9f0f-030820d9bd70}} , {{formula:86b557c8-cdeb-40d9-925b-8a4109feb9d0}} stands for the set of all morphisms {{formula:914e92c0-c9fa-4bc9-9114-2cc603d2a0cb}} ; similarly for {{formula:66aad640-d2d3-4b88-867c-94818b6b6cb4}} , when the composition makes sense. Given categories {{formula:14963ddc-2417-405b-b1bd-69683bad8974}} , we denote the category {{formula:695fabdd-9bcc-4a3f-90dd-8a27b6f308a0}} simply by {{formula:8bce95d8-e71e-43a5-bf29-c854863bb965}} . All functors are covariant, except when explicitly mentioned otherwise. Definition 1.1 Let {{formula:ca2163de-186f-4a19-8b3b-2542ea568df0}} be a complete, cocomplete category. A small category {{formula:b4674c68-2af6-46fb-99fe-a9c237aac6cf}} is said to be {{formula:ef361815-492d-45c0-b54b-692e609e2941}} -Frobenius if the diagonal functor {{formula:950c8ab2-77b6-46dc-b0e0-0530266f8077}} is a Frobenius functor. Remark 1.2 The left adjoint to {{formula:83a271bc-24ad-48d0-a079-7fc078b6552d}} is the functor {{formula:22bc2bdd-d1cd-43d8-8dd8-011fd635e914}} , sending {{formula:e3f54fa8-91d1-4772-a931-e444e9886e69}} to its colimit {{formula:6f3e1583-8e81-45c7-a8c4-8aa8a9fb620d}} . Similarly, the right adjoint to {{formula:8b757f0f-969f-44ef-9267-7ec812c6da75}} is the functor sending {{formula:3657e158-e48a-4e9e-b827-88eb67ade8db}} to its limit {{formula:d15a6ef7-9aff-4b88-8bd7-bb63d534279c}} ({{cite:9a167d9fd4d622832b0843ee9a5656fc06738694}}). Consequently, saying that {{formula:015e833d-5dec-4a74-97ad-191420da205d}} is Frobenius is the same as saying that {{formula:83202025-8796-4f03-a262-710d8765486b}} and {{formula:32253a59-1da7-4c0d-8a17-770894328aaa}} are naturally isomorphic. This means that we can find, for each functor {{formula:51ec517f-187c-43eb-92ca-9ae45e368d6d}} , an isomorphism {{formula:5fd5de4c-52e2-4f63-a299-7814baac3abe}} such that for every natural transformation {{formula:f3b22ea9-5f70-4dc1-aa39-9906541be1f0}} one has the commutative diagram {{formula:a029af4e-dcc2-4405-bd43-59d1c04acec4}} Remark 1.3 Notice that the empty category is {{formula:17b9d382-b88a-4c21-bcff-033986db4a74}} -Frobenius if and only if {{formula:2b1e8ae9-846b-493d-9189-4cfb580bb102}} has a zero object. In order to avoid splitting the arguments into cases, we assume from now on that all our categories are non-empty. We remarked earlier that we would be concerned primarily with the case when {{formula:a108e1c5-6d7d-401f-a918-7a53129e9631}} is connected. In fact, as the following lemma shows, the general problem of finding the {{formula:4e3208c5-9fe6-46cd-8e33-919a7621a19f}} -Frobenius small categories {{formula:53f31d43-052a-48fb-b398-602eee650dc7}} for a given {{formula:f99677fd-3259-4650-8e87-1943e3f2dde1}} breaks up into the connected and the discrete case under certain conditions which do occur in the cases of interest. Lemma 1.4 Let {{formula:d90eb60c-0135-4399-92fe-cb1d6bdcfb32}} be a complete, cocomplete category and {{formula:54c2fa2b-1c6d-41d5-b16e-55054c8109be}} a small category with connected components {{formula:cfef482d-b715-42df-ae36-7e05bb340d9e}} . Then: If each component {{formula:e3917408-6f3e-41c0-9e13-7dc3ac403558}} is {{formula:a69db840-ae78-4b67-957c-7c9c444060bc}} -Frobenius and the set {{formula:719bc378-105b-4e27-beec-eaca8f219d58}} , regarded as a discrete category, is {{formula:de1b223a-cc82-4a51-a517-9ccf3741db5a}} -Frobenius, then {{formula:e2f8bee2-20ce-4420-b31b-db0323a09d9d}} is {{formula:b0883747-db31-4c79-8dc3-779595356ccd}} -Frobenius. If {{formula:de0ce6a5-5e3a-4c1d-a00a-a1f7a852d72d}} is {{formula:7293dc46-18fb-4c4a-8b6c-c736e6c5259d}} -Frobenius, then {{formula:c2cb4581-8f99-4c29-9ee0-6bce083094cd}} is {{formula:8877aea3-9ec6-4df8-966d-ba2d901517e8}} -Frobenius. The converse of {{formula:16b171df-591b-43db-8966-d22a6a889389}} holds if {{formula:31e908df-4145-4dbb-90fb-5babbfb15c4d}} has a zero object. Before proving the three assertions, we make some observations useful in all three arguments. Fix a functor {{formula:ff40d46b-8453-4fed-b278-68c2a12e08a7}} , and consider the contravariant functor {{formula:5c9e00f9-d94f-4bb7-9dcd-dd1a40f10099}} defined by sending each object {{formula:1a48ea18-c673-4d15-b6cb-d0b8ecc6b02c}} to the set of cones {{formula:9380e841-ad93-4066-9b68-5b4a7969e10f}} (Mac Lane's terminology and notation; see {{cite:9a167d9fd4d622832b0843ee9a5656fc06738694}}). The set of cones can also be defined as the object set of the comma category {{formula:7cdb92d2-cf4f-45ec-be7b-3901f96d4701}} ({{cite:9a167d9fd4d622832b0843ee9a5656fc06738694}}). Since {{formula:9e0086a0-87bb-41d5-8326-cd4176ea046d}} is small, the comma category is indeed small, so it makes sense to talk about its object set. Notice that the limit {{formula:6126922d-38c8-4bad-b6d9-9fe6b90d9a05}} is precisely the representing object of {{formula:eaed68e4-b4d7-4d26-966a-b7f6a756ce77}} . Moreover, {{formula:81586afa-e949-4df4-9622-364af895467c}} is natural in {{formula:c1175fc7-661d-44a4-8140-a6fa0b901697}} . On the other hand, again having fixed {{formula:5d3aeca7-26c7-4cda-8537-35123bf4c977}} , consider the functor {{formula:d4e8c21c-5e83-4350-bdae-06b2ee66c7b5}} sending {{formula:7e062dcd-235d-4661-9ab9-8e321e729b0c}} to collections of cones {{formula:c9288635-f6e0-4806-a24e-c246cd96c326}} from {{formula:e411bf86-4e4e-49e1-968d-1111a079f2ed}} to the restrictions of {{formula:c52006a9-f8fc-44d9-8bc0-ebaec21b13a7}} to the connected components {{formula:fccda7e2-536c-48f6-91c6-fcb4705ca099}} . By the definition of limits, the representing object for {{formula:c33604c7-9975-4695-8616-8a01494fa509}} is {{formula:862a904c-bbf8-4b7e-ab63-6acb6ababf24}} . Notice however that, since there are no morphisms between distinct connected components, the functors {{formula:5a108038-6ce1-4ffe-a91f-b60a677afb29}} and {{formula:b2a9d8b4-8477-4a79-a4e9-3bdba13391c9}} actually coincide. In conclusion, the representing objects {{formula:9942e838-6cfa-467a-9cab-1e9fec640361}} and {{formula:35da4a53-e2c8-44a3-9fae-fa74e4114638}} are in fact isomorphic; the isomorphism exhibited here is natural in {{formula:2f5726cf-e8d5-4cd3-acc6-69edf065f54f}} , because {{formula:1dc37fc3-9234-476b-ba85-726164f99775}} is. Similarly, {{formula:5e00b815-08b0-48bf-acc3-12ad4fdb3b06}} . We are now ready for the proof proper. (a) We have just seen that {{formula:274ebeb4-fed5-4f9e-bb0a-d7e363bc7778}} naturally in {{formula:95bf9539-7464-4725-bab4-9f1d3de3cd10}} . Each {{formula:86e76e87-49d7-4f62-ac21-0afc6ef84803}} is Frobenius, so the latter is isomorphic to {{formula:e96525dc-23db-49f2-a13e-a77555dc92e0}} (naturally in {{formula:88028c61-4268-4ea9-ab75-919eedbaf255}} ). The component set {{formula:80044155-a6ba-4590-b0a3-af416049ad27}} is Frobenius, so this is isomorphic to {{formula:5c7139e3-a390-45e3-b37c-e584f9606534}} (again, naturally in {{formula:cf5dc366-5783-428e-b6cb-48d41182ca7d}} ). Finally, the above discussion shows that this is isomorphic to {{formula:8927e74a-a2d6-4ce4-ab79-1c57d3ed7999}} . (b) Instead of looking at the whole of {{formula:46402547-bbc9-47c8-9130-a985a03f2ffc}} , consider only those functors {{formula:69af90db-49b9-489c-98ad-5639ee9d7110}} which restrict to constants on each component {{formula:65286284-9753-4ed0-a231-73d0b86e633d}} . These are precisely the functors factoring through the canonical functor {{formula:489b1396-6a9a-4388-b20b-3f0cc1e1d084}} , which sends each {{formula:51c43398-8f71-4083-8b7c-f177514ea6be}} to {{formula:31db4b39-4766-4abf-817a-a533bf5a783b}} . Again, use the isomorphism {{formula:cdda3bf8-241c-4591-8c57-b092b6ae65b2}} : the limit of a constant functor on a connected category is easily seen to be precisely the image object (with all structural morphisms equal to the identity); it follows that in the case at hand, when {{formula:bbbdd5f7-e752-49b1-bca8-4bc2ec123246}} restricts to a constant on each component, {{formula:a4986bb7-6f5c-4447-bd03-5899c248bedc}} is naturally isomorphic to the product of the objects {{formula:8388b08f-bcad-4651-a531-01ed021233e4}} . The same discussion applies to colimits: {{formula:6209f763-dfac-4c86-80eb-afb56d6e75be}} . The desired conclusion that {{formula:feb8cb38-2ede-4952-808b-0659a2495f2f}} must be {{formula:ae72f682-60a4-4896-b92f-2501d1c7ea50}} -Frobenius follows. (c) In view of (b), we must show that given the additional hypothesis of a zero object, each {{formula:c582e79a-b90e-4915-b607-221dab0f56bf}} is {{formula:daa66c1a-2f68-4b13-b0d5-d9c616d3a764}} -Frobenius. section_text: limitations. This section will examine the loss of information if other that optimal filtering is used. It may be less than optimal in that it is not matched, e.g., an all analog filter, or in that the pass band is optimized for another condition. {{figure:c18842fd-5aa0-43e0-bba9-7b4224813c16}} Let us look at the case of an all analog filter. In this case all filtering is done prior to digitizing and the only digital processing performed is interpolation. I will take the B A B AR TDR design (described in subsection REF ). This has a charge sensitive preamp followed by a CR and then two RC filters. Together these give the equivalent of three RC filters, all with the corner frequency {{formula:3076e316-63c4-4aad-8d43-ab91a97b0d2f}} . This has the transfer function {{formula:ef1af49c-ed50-40e3-87ee-7f8fff6871fb}} The signal is {{formula:8553d735-7ee5-49d7-98c3-ca8458626fb6}} {{figure:8a4d5987-9c52-491d-b42f-4def3d9d2a29}} The time dependence of the output signal is given by the inverse Fourier transform of their product. This integral can be done by contour integration. If the contour is completed by a semi-circle at infinity around the upper half plane (for {{formula:8576437f-d16d-4d07-b062-88cb0d29c06a}} ), the integral can be deduced from the residues at the poles {{formula:3244b28d-89d3-4032-b2bf-03aa0da9d256}} and {{formula:1f52eaf9-d323-4805-8452-2d1de5015143}} . The result is {{formula:61c13493-7c00-485d-936e-5e04056d6250}} This is shown for several time constants in figure REF . The peak value vs. time constant is shown in figure REF . Since there are no poles in the lower half plane, the integral is 0 for {{formula:4bd9fa70-f632-496b-96b5-450449fcb801}} . {{figure:db82b102-c07c-4122-8e17-c3c3584f5a72}} The mean square noise is given by the inverse Fourier transform of the noise evaluated at {{formula:966a78b7-864b-4df3-b6cd-f71329a9c2a2}} , i.e., the autocorrelation for no time difference. The noise before filtering is given by equation REF . The mean square noise is {{formula:b9b66665-a7fd-4ff8-80c1-bcf04f605f4b}} The contribution of the electronic noise is {{formula:56f0a6fb-54d2-4655-ad60-1d2380592936}} The peak of {{formula:94e343ca-3a64-479d-b4ac-57d4ef45e23f}} gives the ENC for the electronic noise after analog filtering. Appropriate scaling gives the ENE shown in Figure REF . The background noise contribution is {{formula:8c0d55bf-e81e-42af-8870-d954bbb8f8a6}} {{formula:1b4cc9f6-7cb4-42cf-b567-20ecefa8b5ab}} is given by their sum. The signal to noise ratio for a single sample taken at time {{formula:50c6c3b9-1e23-4c7d-8bd7-344523df1544}} is given by {{formula:fc3e9c11-7bce-4e33-8974-bd8ec61f179b}} . If we divide this by the optimum signal to noise given by equation we get the “efficiency” for this single sample versus the sample time. Figure REF shows this function for the B A B AR calorimeter during nominal operating conditions for several values of the corner frequency. The highest efficiency achieved is 68% for a shaping time constant of 0.2{{formula:bc5dfb84-6e53-4b36-bf34-ac87698467d9}} . For low background conditions (Figure REF ) the peak efficiency is 80% at a shaping time of 1.5{{formula:756e5375-ffba-4821-b94a-17c9e9b4583e}} . At ten times nominal background, (Figure REF ) the efficiency drops to 50% at a shaping time of 0.12{{formula:331a7ff4-a557-40d4-8f1b-7196ed41566f}} . The loss of efficiency for nominal and better background conditions is not significant. The loss at during high background conditions hits just when noise is the causing the most problems. Matched filters utilize knowledge of the signal shape. In low background conditions, the optimum shaping time is longer than the signal. The shape of the signal is not seen and matched filters offer little advantage. The situation and conclusions are reversed in high background conditions. The cost of using an analog filter optimized for conditions other than those encountered is more dramatic. If the corner frequency is set to the 0.2{{formula:254121a9-8acf-4f86-9387-328092ce54ad}} which is optimal for nominal conditions, but the backgrounds are actually at {{formula:16be1f16-1a42-4512-bc90-fd218fb09a55}} nominal levels, the efficiency is 44%. If the corner frequency were optimal for low background conditions, the efficiency at {{formula:7b1fd292-6df1-4ee7-abfc-837169c16b2a}} nominal background would be 12%. Since the important conclusions may have gotten lost in the derivations, I'll review them here. Machine background can be treated as a current noise with the spectrum of the signal. The best possible amplitude and time measurements can be obtained with a matched filter. The errors in the amplitude and time are not correlated, therefore knowing the time does not improve the ultimate precision of the amplitude determination, although such knowledge may reduce the computation required. The signal to noise methodology used here reproduces previous results. The background current noise dominates the photodiode shot noise even at nominal backgrounds and in the quietest part of the calorimeter. For nominal background where {{formula:0534bc03-fd8c-4526-a215-f5ec9f9be65e}} : {{formula:9dd309a8-fdf5-4441-82f8-5e039984a00e}} The sampling frequency of 3.7{{formula:2ead62fd-31ee-4fa6-b0cf-8d4a2251894c}} is adequate at nominal backgraounds, but it is marginal for {{formula:d8f38aa0-7a14-4c20-ab6a-b3c630c4ac64}} nominal background levels. At this frequency, 64 samples will have to be processed under nominal conditions. The step of an ADC bit (on the most sensitive range) should be set so that there are at least 13 bits to full scale (12{{formula:3a37df63-8a4c-4862-80c5-58b138700158}} ) during nominal background. For quiet conditions and with a differentiating stage in the analog filter, 16.5 bits may be required. Simple analog filters can achieve near optimal results in low to moderate background conditions if the shaping time is optimized for the actual conditions. heading: Conclusion and Future Directions
section_text:
We provided tractable solutions to a variety of finite-horizon stochastic optimal control problems with quadratic cost, hard control constraints, and unbounded additive noise. These problems arise as parts of solutions to the stochastic receding horizon problems (REF ). The control policy obtained as a result of the finite-horizon optimal control sub-problems may be nonlinear with respect to the previous states, and the policy elements are chosen from a vector space that is largely up to the designer. One of the key features of our approach is that the variance-like matrices employed in the finite-horizon optimal control sub-problems may be computed off-line, and we illustrated this feature with several examples. We demonstrated that applying our obtained policies in a receding horizon fashion results in bounded state variance. Finally, we provided several numerical examples that illustrate the effectiveness of our method with respect to the commonly used certainty-equivalent MPC controllers.
The development in this article affords extensions in several directions. One is the incorporation of state constraints. As discussed in §, hard state constraints do not make sense in the stochastic with additive unbounded noise setting unless one is prepared to artificially relax them once infeasibility is encountered. Probabilistic constraints and integrated chance constraints {{cite:707f5978df8bf1386689907fe6a42b0cb1ef9cf1}} constitute popular alternative methods to impose constraints on the state that are more probabilistic in nature. It will be interesting to see how the approach introduced in this article reacts to state-constraints. A second direction is to consider specific kinds of nonlinear models, particularly those which involve multiplicative noise, in our framework, and a third is to consider different objective functions such as affine functions given by the {{formula:70ef0204-9ee1-43ab-8dd1-ecb99d4fb2c6}}  and the {{formula:98ce4587-a2cc-431e-8781-ba8a85146ed7}}  norms.

heading: The most severe limitation of our study is that the high-resolution
section_text:
simulations used here include only dark matter. Without baryons,
these haloes are sub-critical (see §) and
incapable of producing multiple images. We are therefore forced to
incorporate a model for the baryonic galaxy at the centre of each
halo. The galaxy changes not only the overall dark matter profiles
(taken into account by adiabatic contraction), but also the
dynamical evolution of subhaloes, an effect which is not considered
here. On the one hand, the increased baryonic density at the centre
of the halo will make the subhaloes feel stronger tidal forces,
particularly those that come close to the centre. On the other hand,
the baryons within subhaloes will make them more resilient to tidal
disruption. It is not clear which effect will dominate. We comment,
however, that the subhaloes that come very close to the centre may
have already been tidally stripped or disrupted, and thus most of
the surviving subhaloes that can be identified by SUBFIND may
have quite large peri-centre passages. As a result, the effects of
baryons in the host halo may not change the results very
significantly. However, we caution that, SUBFIND, like most
substructure finders, has difficulties in identifying subhaloes in
the densest regions of the halo and assigning them correct masses.

heading: Our conclusion that the dark matter subhalo population may be
section_text:
insufficient to explain the observed cusp violations is consistent
with {{cite:444b0fb1d1abdd6fab909915490dc5afd8f46e8a}}, {{cite:2b74d9b670c8060131ceb16dee1a3c184c42a308}}, {{cite:b4d6f27caecb80380204b0a4fa87883abf290e1c}}
and {{cite:e2aa4483d22eaefd2d01b16b42cb926db1c1622e}}. The number of particles used in those studies
is roughly two orders of magnitude smaller than here. In particular,
the study by {{cite:444b0fb1d1abdd6fab909915490dc5afd8f46e8a}} found large scatter among different
haloes, a conclusion confirmed by our results.

heading: Future work includes investigating more general topologies for
section_text:
network coding-based protection. The 2+1 scheme can be viewed as
one where there is usually no sharing of protection resources
between different primary connections, whereas the 4+n scheme
enforces full sharing of the protection resources. Schemes that
exhibit a tradeoff between these two are worth investigating. For example, one could consider provisioning two primary paths for each connection, instead of one and design corresponding network coding protocols. This would reduce the number of protection paths one needs to provision, and depending on the network topology, potentially have a lower cost. It
is also interesting to further examine the resource savings when
we partition the primary paths into subsets and provision
protection resources for each subset separately. Furthermore, in
this paper we considered an adversarial error model. When errors
are random, we could use classical error control codes to provide
protection. But it is interesting to consider schemes that combine
channel coding across time and the coding across the protection
paths in a better manner. A reviewer has pointed out that rank
metric codes {{cite:19d40165ce54db81422af5ff247c238b5a8899c3}} might be also useful for this
problem.

section_text: limitations on the shortest track that can be observed leading to combinatoric ambiguities identifying decay products from new particle states that are created and decay at the “effective" vertex of the collision. Any new physics discovered will come with unknown couplings, mixing angles, spins, interactions, and masses. One approach is to assume a model and fit the model parameters to the observed data. However, we have hundreds of distinct anticipated theories possessing tens of new particle states with differing spins and couplings each with tens of parameters. Global fits to approximately {{formula:38435cd9-4c70-4ec9-9da3-651aa0c35ed0}} events recorded per year are an enormous amount of work, and assume that the `correct model' has been anticipated. We would like to measure the particle properties with minimal model assumptions. The term `model-independent' technique is misleading because we are always assuming some model. When we say model-independent, we mean that we assume broadly applicable assumptions such as special relativity. We also try to ensure that our techniques are largely independent of a priori unknown coupling coefficients and model parameters. For this reason our desire for model-independence constrains our toolbox to kinematic properties of particle production and decay. If we are able to determine the mass of the dark-matter particle, other properties follow more easily. Knowing the dark-matter particle's mass, the remaining mass spectrum follows from kinematic edges. If we know the dark-matter's mass and gluino's mass, then the sign of the gluino's mass predicted in Chapter can be determined from the distribution of the invariant mass of jet pairs from the decay of gluino pair production {{cite:92abdea21814887b891de4785932d7003e228f12}}. Another avenue to the sign of the gluino's mass requires measuring the masses of the gluino and the two stop squarks and the measuring the decay width of gluino to these states {{cite:ea40f4daf3ed6338906708699e20ed24b80e9d9f}}. In addition, the measurement of spin correlations, a study that can contribute to spin determination, has historically relied on knowing the masses to reconstruct the event kinematics {{cite:4b80d956a6ff9e1d9e6501282afd145c93cc3565}}. In short, mass determination is a key part to identifying the underlying theory which lies beyond the Standard Model. Newly discovered particles could be Kaluza-Klein (KK) states from extra-dimensions, supersymmetric partners of known states, technicolor hadrons, or something else that we have not anticipated. Models predict relationships between parameters. Supersymmetry relates the couplings of current fermions to the couplings of new bosons, and the supersymmetric particle masses reflect the origin of supersymmetry breaking. Masses of KK states tell us about the size of the extra dimensions. If these parameters, such as the masses and spins, can be measured without assuming the model, then these observations exclude or confirm specific models. In general, mass determination of new particle states is central to discerning what lies beyond the Standard Model. If dark matter is produced at a hadron collider, the likely signature will be missing transverse momentum. The lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) or lightest Kaluza-Klein particle (LKP) is expected to be neutral, stable, and invisible to the particle detectors. The astrophysical dark matter appears to be stable. Whatever symmetry makes dark matter stable and / or distinguishes superpartners from their Standard-Model cousins will likely also require that dark matter particles be pair produced. Therefore, events with supersymmetric new particle states are expected to end in two LSP's leaving the detector unnoticed. Events with Kaluza-Klien particles are expected to end with two LKP's leaving the detector unnoticed. The presence of two invisible particles prevents complete reconstruction of the kinematics of any single event and leads to missing transverse momentum in the events. At a hadron collider, because the partons colliding each carry an unknown fraction of the hadron's momentum we do not know the reference frame of the collision. Although the individual parton momentum is unknown, the statistical distribution of the parton's momentum can be measured from deep inelastic scattering {{cite:45b9c35a4369a03ce4c3a5b152a009aac2625155}}. The measured parton distribution functions (PDFs) {{formula:21dcf6ac-c8ca-4cae-9a34-9c233fe7f9a9}} give the distribution of parton {{formula:e94f61fc-531a-47b5-b53a-7699beab18d1}} within the hadron {{formula:bf1b4887-7dbe-44f1-a32d-dc511f2d77da}} carrying {{formula:a0df72d1-9d5f-4a8c-a663-f1a84df4855d}} fraction of the hadron's momentum when probed by a space-like momentum probe {{formula:bc177d07-567e-4171-bd26-b62b1ef78ef6}} with {{formula:469535bd-1d3c-481b-bf16-391c66372c67}} . {{formula:a3794fd2-ab09-4758-bacd-5afa7c701ac4}} is also the factorization scale at which one cuts off collinear divergences. The dominant parton types {{formula:164a3b7c-019e-42e6-bc1c-ef1c4b464120}} are {{formula:c5570e06-14f6-49d1-aca3-c4e576919f5a}} , {{formula:9d6733bc-4aa8-40c4-8011-1110b52bdbfd}} , {{formula:b7c71052-a5d2-414d-9534-9803e64f5552}} , their antiparticles {{formula:d456708b-0597-4546-8f2d-5688a8d83b67}} , {{formula:ca3b70d7-73de-46e7-b6b9-440b6cb7a0ae}} , {{formula:46179004-9087-47e4-93f2-61c033ba1b41}} , and gluons {{formula:2e5847a4-d107-48b1-8f55-ee6ee72cf30e}} . The events produced in the collider follow from a convolution of the cross section over the parton distribution functions. If the two colliding protons have 4-momentum {{formula:546cc3cb-884d-43ae-9fcf-f97e700d3945}} and {{formula:eaa9f02c-454e-495f-a28c-93720f6abaee}} , then for example the {{formula:2f83f311-a6f2-482f-be56-e3de07fd8e72}} and {{formula:1538373e-af2b-4f3a-a65d-f9effa2a835e}} quarks colliding would have 4-momentum {{formula:4addd031-e0bc-46cd-9003-ecd5f0f19a4e}} and {{formula:85499e79-c085-4aa6-bc62-42c6cd2372a4}} . The spatial momentum of the collision along the beam axis is given by {{formula:f30bd112-c632-4392-bc17-25cbf98d6653}} , and the center-of-mass energy of the parton collision is {{formula:30f1ba3d-797a-43ce-ac8e-458030dd918a}} . Because {{formula:28738259-f471-482c-aae8-2bf379d85a99}} and {{formula:8340d435-b7b0-4230-8da7-74eee298068d}} are only known statistically, any individual collision has an unknown center-of-mass energy and an unknown momentum along the beam axis. LHC processes are calculated by convolutions over the PDFs as in {{formula:3fbee32b-c72d-4afd-a575-f5dfb611441d}} where {{formula:882acfe0-ba0c-409b-9f40-2ae8fab2c754}} is the total cross section for a given parton collision center-of-mass squared {{formula:4e71d2f8-8a65-4969-a9ab-9552e6e564e6}} , factorization scale {{formula:43ffb3eb-ed3c-4a4a-a6f3-b2a272d2b90b}} , and {{formula:ddc974c6-00d3-447d-8f89-44729754e881}} is the center-of-mass collision energy of the protons colliding at the LHC. The region of integration of {{formula:7eeb508b-3c01-4939-8399-073635da34d4}} and {{formula:6b9dd3ce-16cf-46de-8421-2340dcd6d119}} is based on the kinematically allowable regions. The factorization scale {{formula:45d24c4b-a802-4c70-97be-6c0e84c07e2e}} is chosen to minimize the size of the logarithms associated with regulating collinear divergences in the cross section. See Ref {{cite:685ae985cfc13ab8c49fb875454f747e6bf0e5f1}} for a recent review on choosing the factorization scale. Calculating these input cross sections even at tree

No further changes need be made to Adv's buffer as RG also sends {{formula:68c95a68-ae03-4b0e-a61d-7fbe7b09088a}} . Thus in this case the adversary's expected gain is {{formula:00228744-26d2-4ac5-af13-01ba106b624d}} . We have shown that, as long as the adversary is oblivious, the ideas of Li et al. {{cite:7dea4b903be4da72f90bb017b8160de130d3a1ab}} can be applied to randomized algorithms, and devised a {{formula:20958963-9b50-41bf-98da-2991fa12affb}} -competitive algorithm this way. section_text: conclusion and future work expectation. Soft fault analysis is based on soft fault injection. At a random moment of the encryption machine's driving procedure, the attacker changes the values of some random positions of the state. By the differential of the key–stream, the attacker can obtain several additional low–degree–equations of the state. Hard fault analysis is based on hard fault injection. The attacker makes the values of some random positions of the state permanently 0. That is, after hard fault injection, those injected bits can be read out as 0, but can no longer be written in. According to technical restriction, hard fault injection must be made before the encryption machine's driving procedure. Three comparisons between hard fault analysis and soft fault analysis are as follows. Comparison 1: Hard fault analysis is more practical than soft fault analysis. The main criticism against soft fault analysis was the transient fault model that was claimed to be unrealistic {{cite:92b340c75cd22d9426391e4d54b09378c52b852a}}. Hard fault injection is a current technique for micro–probing, and has already become real danger to cipher chip {{cite:02305016d4f4c914ab38899f9b51bce0c7ae6f92}}. For example, DS5003 is a new product of Maxim. It is a secure microprocessor chip by using coating technique, for resisting hard fault injection. Comparison 2: Hard fault analysis is more expensive than soft fault analysis. section_text: open question about this work is whether or not we can guarantee convergence. Empirically, by initializing belief propagation to various random points in the feasible space, we found BP still converged to the same solution. The max-product algorithm is guaranteed to converge to the correct maximum matching {{cite:62c3835f60a7d9d0455781936880ae6518e86115}}, {{cite:fb4e51cff3f66ca5cfcd0497a27cc2d6a4d127b5}} via arguments on the unwrapped computation tree of belief propagation. The matching graphical model does not not meet the sufficient conditions provided in {{cite:0de2fc4fa723c06e1a54315104d41e8b9768d839}} nor does our distribution fit the criteria for non-convex convergence provided in {{cite:b81ff7c45c69aa9347e5ff04054e1a3c96285951}} and {{cite:7b4e3d57565a28373aef1fc2c618e15f71bd0f94}}. In our analysis, we have found that the Bethe free energy is certainly non-convex near the vertices of the distribution. That is, if we evaluate the Bethe free energy on pseudomarginals corresponding to exactly one matching, and take a tiny step in the direction of a non-adjacent matching vertex, Bethe free energy increases. On the other hand, when we initialize belief propagation such that the beliefs are at a vertex, BP moves away from the apparent local minimum and converges to the same solution as other initializations. This behavior implies that, while the Bethe free energy within the matching constraints is non-convex, it may still have a unique zero-gradient point despite not fitting the criteria in {{cite:7b4e3d57565a28373aef1fc2c618e15f71bd0f94}}, which exploit the strength of potentials. Since all our empirical evidence implies that BP always converges, we suspect that we have not yet correctly analyzed the true space traversed during optimization. In particular, the distribution described by Equation REF is defined over the set of all {{formula:264e57e9-3d6c-4175-abd1-420d3e9a495c}} possible {{formula:381e759c-763f-4dda-8250-b0b3dd3f6937}} states, while it is only nonzero in {{formula:c1976eb7-309a-4ad5-bd75-a990c0b85a96}} states. Any beliefs derived from belief propagation obey similar constraints, so it is reasonable to suspect that careful analysis of the optimization with special attention to the oddities of the distribution could yield more promising theoretical guarantees. However, without being rigorous, we can note that the matching constraints created by the {{formula:0ece980e-471d-452d-bce3-14c7635573ac}} functions enforce that the singleton beliefs are exactly the matched pairwise beliefs. This means we can think of these as entries in a doubly-stochastic matrix {{formula:4fc8ad31-9ae0-4c8c-a5ca-dd01d7b39a0f}} . {{formula:b6af2339-0100-4460-af98-40d5022cd266}} Therefore it becomes clear that there is a strong connection to the Sinkhorn operation {{cite:62154ccc3407d19976000bd077255ec74f1e18e3}}, which iteratively scales rows and columns of a matrix until it converges to a doubly-stochastic matrix. It has been shown that the Sinkhorn operation effectively minimizes the pseudo-KL divergence between some matrix and the doubly-stochastic matrix{{cite:67846e2fc9555c9fedfc50d09c2be15766bf1d8b}}. {{formula:13475dda-3e51-40de-aed9-2a451d4e52ab}} Here the pseudo-KL divergence can be interpreted as the KL for each row and each column, each of which is an assignment distribution like in our matching setting. The Sinkhorn procedure is guaranteed to converge for indecomposable input matrices {{cite:62154ccc3407d19976000bd077255ec74f1e18e3}}, so the fact that the the procedure is reminiscent of ours is encouraging. However the two procedures differ enough that the guarantee does not directly translate. {{figure:c3aec78d-d76f-490b-b44b-1e646689fcd8}} In this section we evaluate the performance of this algorithm in terms of running time and accuracy, and finally we exemplify a possible usage of the approximate permanent as a kernel function. We ran belief propagation to approximate the permanents of random matrices of sizes {{formula:80d783ba-23a1-4530-bdc2-88a605ea62f2}} , recording the total running time and the number of iterations to convergence. Surprisingly, the number of iterations to convergence initially decreased as {{formula:39c7f417-5b47-4c08-a217-b90f8fb3b865}} grew, but appears to remain constant beyond {{formula:8c1097e0-ec3e-4ee0-9d38-974fedf2ec9b}} or so. Running time still increased because the cost of updating each iteration well subsumes the decrease in iterations to convergence. In our implementation, we checked for convergence by computing the absolute change in all the messages from the previous iteration, and considered the algorithm converged if the sum of all the changes of all {{formula:5cf7e672-f15a-49fe-889e-edf9ba712a84}} messages was less than {{formula:5875c1cc-0e9e-4c90-b2ee-308a414b3f35}} . In all cases, the resulting beliefs were consistent with each other within comparable precision to our convergence threshold. These experiments were run on a a 2.4 Ghz Intel Core 2 Duo Apple Macintosh running Mac OS X 10.5. The code is in {{formula:2cbfdfbc-a3ce-4bc3-94c3-f89c6b85695d}} and compiled using gcc version 4.0.1. {{table:87e16267-a670-4428-9292-b1778f8bf064}}{{figure:9d3a9ab8-800f-4799-9357-dd269667c479}} We evaluate the accuracy of our algorithm by creating 1000 random matrices of sizes 5, 8 and 200 matrices of size 10. The entries of each of these matrices were randomly drawn from a uniform distribution in the interval {{formula:2efc2f57-4cca-4409-9204-b8ea016dc92b}} . We computed the true permanents of these matrices, then computed approximate permanents using our Bethe approximation. We also computed an approximate using a naive sampling method, where we sample by choosing random permutations and storing a cumulative sum of each permutation's corresponding product. We sampled for the same amount of actual time our belief propagation algorithm took to converge. Finally we also computed two weak approximations: the determinant and the scaled product of the diagonal entries. In order to be able to compare to the true permanent, we had to limit this analysis to small matrices. However, since MCMC sampling methods such as in {{cite:1dce6b8001f05e652b5f12ceea15bbd2a6236bcb}} take {{formula:4e3d27ea-1a04-4a95-8b78-0bef0f08ac0d}} time to reach less than some {{formula:b214eabe-3f94-40a1-9dd2-0865391c61a8}} error, as matrix size increases, the precision achievable in comparable time to our algorithm would decrease. We scale the cumulative sum by {{formula:b2c25d9d-69f1-4011-95e5-21c13d7755aa}} , where {{formula:eb25278b-e952-4373-87f3-6184ad2d5145}} is the number of samples. This is the ratio of the total possible permutations and the number of samples. In our experiments, determinants and the products of diagonals are neither accurate nor consistent approximations of the permanent. Sampling, however, is accurate with respect to absolute distance to the permanent, so for applications where that is most important, it may be best to apply some sort of sampling method.

Hence, the above theorem tells us that just the expansion properties of {{formula:0eb20259-188d-44fe-98ae-9d57408ba2bc}} for any {{formula:fefc2ec0-6184-4b2d-9ada-45bdb1339d64}} -sized {{formula:96a2b9b0-9e0b-4596-8864-a2ee75a500f6}} are not sufficient to guarantee {{formula:21241505-b610-40e0-a02d-22bc5f748bf5}} -distance from every subspace of dimension {{formula:cedc48f1-b440-4f22-8371-1af351f21004}} . The proof of the above statement can be found in the full version {{cite:e7a8aa36305e25a2ab566aaa39efc22dbd4b1126}}. For the remote point problem over an Abelian group {{formula:985a009d-bd62-484b-9edf-35ec3e04a7d1}} , we have shown how expanding generating sets for Cayley graphs of {{formula:f888182c-0214-4f30-8a8d-1d4603ed5540}} can be used to obtain deterministic {{formula:599ba2b1-1724-4975-b408-e84520b7b89b}} algorithms. A natural question is whether we can obtain a similar algorithm for non-Abelian {{formula:2c770f8d-509c-45ee-b2e2-63316fa78021}} . Note that Lemma holds in the non-Abelian setting too. Hence, in order to obtain an {{formula:5298deca-0468-4145-b0fe-f1cd4d3efcb8}} -algorithm for the RPP over arbitrary non-Abelian {{formula:e748a801-bed2-46d7-906f-be3d02706592}} along the lines of our algorithm for Abelian groups, we need to be able to check (in {{formula:ee239f59-7a7a-4137-9cba-9598ad5a1ae3}} ) for membership in {{formula:fbb6fe3e-bb6d-415f-8bdc-6f9979605660}} , and we need to be able to construct small multisets {{formula:b2f7e1d8-1eec-4f36-8f09-415c27792270}} of {{formula:ebb97811-de24-481e-a6a9-cd06558140aa}} such that {{formula:2f16dd6e-79bf-416b-a916-c043ced96ba6}} has sufficiently good expansion properties. Luks' work {{cite:7405a07de8de7b5c905131a4ecf04f1b69d15884}} yields an {{formula:a9be3a54-4011-4310-8566-cef6be2e4c14}} test for membership in {{formula:276f24b3-ef10-47af-934f-b8aa5a97930a}} for arbitrary {{formula:b56551d8-5ac4-4649-a41d-7150ad1012bb}} . Building on that, there is also an {{formula:eaef66cc-072c-4c71-a04d-50df54d92f10}} membership test for {{formula:f181c23c-150e-43be-b971-1b9460b2063b}} {{cite:7e61923ef17dc256799a4a9c7e0ef8676c412f2b}}. However, we are unable to compute a (good enough) expanding generator set for the group {{formula:29af2a8b-db8b-4381-b55a-ee8ef69a39bd}} in deterministic {{formula:33474645-2853-4724-9087-13e40e4b366b}} or even in deterministic polynomial time. We are grateful to Noga Alon and Sergey Yekhanin for interesting comments. In particular, Alon pointed out to us that Lemma has an alternative proof using the expander mixing lemma. We thank the anonymous referees for their comments and suggestions.
