The following Lemma proceeds exactly as in {{cite:71caf217c0b2b5fa9acfdd1cd1707ac739ba40b5}}. Lemma 3.2 A particular min-cut in G is produced by the contraction algorithm with probability {{formula:6590a4af-9806-4164-b3a4-4532e637f26d}} . Let {{formula:6f517fd0-0de4-465f-a222-1b694bcfd34a}} be the value of the mincut in {{formula:2007ceb9-86c8-4fb0-b0e0-e0afde69f79a}} . Each contraction reduces the number of vertices in the graph by one. Consider the contraction executed when the graph has {{formula:b1f8e550-e917-4bb0-84ca-5e85a099f888}} vertices. Since the contracted graph has a min-cut of at least {{formula:76cc00bb-fb2d-4356-865c-a6ad2824055b}} , it must have minimum degree {{formula:2ea957dd-1d82-444a-b73b-1213f4156b59}} , and thus atleast {{formula:5e79e702-9f1a-4575-b0c4-10f076190dd7}} edges. However, only {{formula:5225dd0f-9537-4128-bff2-fee7a6983b1c}} of these edges are in min-cut. Thus, a randomly chosen edge is in the min-cut with probability at most {{formula:1cb5c51a-2119-4e6b-a780-39ac2061a77e}} . The probability that we never contract a min-cut edge through all {{formula:90f4f174-b103-47e4-813d-15700ff6e00a}} contractions is atleast {{formula:0647c7c0-9aa9-40fa-809b-40e82749e8e1}} Theorem 4.1 The Karger's distributed algorithm uses {{formula:734bb21b-e58c-44df-ab72-dcbf4e47f029}} messages, in a single trial. It is not hard to see that the most expensive steps in a trial are those of determination of {{formula:0f279028-17cf-4618-89ae-2e61ca547383}} from local maxranks(find-global-maxrank()) and that of computing the mincut at the end(find-global-mincut()). In find-global-maxrank(), each node sends its local maxrank value to its neighbours and this is repeated atmost {{formula:d2b3aa32-2572-4a0a-9a8c-a370a0b538e7}} times(number of times equal to the diameter of the graph sufficies). Hence the total number of messages is bounded by {{formula:021afade-de52-4b2a-add1-a133c4c8989d}} . Thus the message complexity for {{formula:9fca2b24-b5d7-4f08-a9e2-03f8388008c9}} iterations per trial is {{formula:f9d23f20-2ec8-4d43-a4e9-f61ab8805198}} . Finally, in step {{formula:1d0ea785-35f8-4756-abf8-49cbdac418cb}} of find-global-mincut(), {{formula:38d64d4f-ca81-4782-ac4a-6121b7e5f546}} nodes send messages to its neighbours. The total number of messages sent at each step is bounded by {{formula:efdd89db-3467-4096-9f42-07265ef95a4d}} . Thus, the total number of messages is {{formula:a5c59ecc-cb8c-4491-ae92-74874ab972c7}} . Hence the overall message complexity is {{formula:446b14e9-43b9-44de-acca-75bb0353e83a}} . Theorem 4.2 The Karger's distributed algorithm computes mincut in {{formula:e5b85085-658c-424f-93ca-b9d71aa4f1b4}} time, in a single trial. Before contraction, the algorithm assigns a rank (random number) to each edge and finds the max-rank among all the vertices in the graph. This requires atmost {{formula:cf6b0e75-6d84-45f2-bc61-2e6f6390b432}} steps(strictly, number of steps equal to the diameter of the graph). For contraction, a message is sent from a vertex within one group to other group and the message is propagated to all the vertices within the second group and the neighbouring vertices of that group, which also takes atmost {{formula:2d4510f6-320c-49bf-9a20-7273d67ca633}} pulses. Since only one contraction can take place at any time and there are {{formula:31343565-2b4e-49bf-8694-76e08c938808}} such contractions, the running time is {{formula:c2f55877-09f1-4a1c-9d4f-999740ca9269}} . To estimate time for computing the mincut, the function find-global-mincut() runs {{formula:382dbcd9-4f0d-4023-8c7a-dea3a1c2359f}} steps and in step {{formula:455a10a5-17d4-473f-9139-2f6b16f837ef}} , {{formula:2e8d28b0-f991-4b8a-b54c-97f1ab71131b}} nodes flood the network. Thus the time per step is {{formula:5acfb40a-50d4-4fd5-89da-1557f1d3ee3b}} . Hence the total complexity is {{formula:0645cf28-97c0-45e6-ab46-77798df5208e}} . A synchronous distributed version of the Karger's randomized algorithm under network setting is presented in this paper with a proof of correctness and complexity analysis. The present algorithm appears not to make use of the full power of parallelism available. It is interesting to look at how to efficiently reduce time and message complexity by conducting edge contractions in parallel.

Thus, we found a {{formula:191b7064-1012-4d9c-987a-2692459b6216}} -partition {{formula:14cd7842-c5d9-4af0-8657-3b89e8820bb8}} with {{formula:8cc54811-a468-4c12-bf98-fa74d834dd9d}} elements and an injective {{formula:84360d6c-6f42-445a-8375-a063f1d932e1}} -automatic presentation {{formula:b5d6c5fd-97c8-41b4-8cc2-6431b30ac508}} such that {{formula:20a40fa4-74a5-4647-b4e6-a9dfe7b6dbc3}} has sets {{formula:286f5208-9f6a-4431-af42-21fbc4abc289}} and {{formula:cf3c3c72-2959-431a-8ed1-5601e2c02456}} in {{formula:8e53a35d-7d10-44d4-af6c-efe7d67adff1}} of size {{formula:db253eaa-46f0-47b9-ac8a-69d5bf1aae15}} with {{formula:e4fb57dc-8415-4f3b-bba4-2e096a22e117}} for {{formula:26086e34-0766-4bcc-aa0d-3ba468ef7b25}} . There is no {{formula:42936bab-9433-4109-b8c5-6e26667b0f63}} -language {{formula:a3ecad88-6634-4f95-a62b-412151a2d0a7}} with {{formula:adf600cb-9dc1-4efd-9f93-62b243903706}} such that {{formula:652ebd7d-9850-4dd6-b3b0-de25db441b01}} is homogeneous of size {{formula:9d6cf9fd-116e-43a4-952d-efdbb9313162}} . Since all context-free {{formula:763da72f-717d-45d3-9acc-d3911d9a274b}} -languages belong to {{formula:cdf52240-62b1-49e8-bf83-0cdd2522e1de}} , the following theorem follows the same way that Lemma REF implied Theorem REF . For all {{formula:8c80fee8-b134-4958-a047-8167a02138f9}} and {{formula:54bb20fc-fe06-4e54-a9ff-97af71b7efc2}} , we have {{formula:051ddbef-fef6-496e-9360-3243559aaa3a}} and {{formula:5c722edc-bbdb-47f2-b8b9-c4f7a684b141}} . This result can be understood as another Sierpiński theorem for {{formula:22654e1d-f53b-4c9d-88ca-7bce4d07d382}} -automatic {{formula:7bfe29d1-8247-42d0-bf3a-3bd3358caf56}} -partitions. This time, it holds for all {{formula:d9c7f00f-c018-4425-9c80-2e8743575dbd}} (not only for {{formula:5f0b6c42-1d17-4af1-9210-83b8822eddd1}} as Theorem REF ). The price to be paid for this is the restriction of homogeneous sets to “simple” ones. In particular the non-existence f regular homogeneous sets provides a Sierpiński theorem in the spirit of automatic structures. Our positive result Theorem REF guarantees the existence of some clique or anticlique of size {{formula:6245c918-5e41-4a64-bba7-2750d3bb53bb}} (and such a clique or anticlique can even be constructed). But the following situation is conceivable: the {{formula:f204aec9-36fa-4a1a-b7f8-4978ed7ba1dc}} -automatic graph contains large cliques without containing large cliques that can be described by a language from {{formula:193efa39-70aa-493a-95cc-888d114803bb}} . In particular, it is not clear whether the existence of a large clique is decidable. A related question concerns Ramsey quantifiers. Rubin {{cite:6db33a0f7cd99de03f15f2274c60f186f93e9151}} has shown that the set of nodes of an automatic graph whose neighbors contain an infinite anticlique is regular (his result is much more general, but this formulation suffices for our purpose). It is not clear whether this also holds for {{formula:87088fb6-b8bf-41e1-b899-533d35738a56}} -automatic graphs. A positive answer to this second question (assuming that it is effective) would entail an affirmative answer to the decidability question above.

section_text: future directions of our work. We list some necessary tables and formulae in appendices. For the anomalous part of the chiral Lagrangian, the leading nontrivial order is {{formula:d50c82d7-d3ef-4cb9-a1bc-82d373d7985a}} and it is the well known Wess-Zumino-Witten term. In Ref.{{cite:6b930fed56923262cdf370343c8b60c7e7f3c383}}, we have calculated the action (REF ) by several different methods and all obtain the same Wess-Zumino-Witten term. If we naively apply these methods to the next to leading order {{formula:92ddb648-b031-4e3f-b8f1-7ad5722c0de8}} computations, we will find that they are too complex to be achieved even with the help of the computer. In this section, we build a method which is suitable to be generalized to the order {{formula:88080616-8727-42a3-942a-03ebb2ef511e}} calculations. The order {{formula:63dd1dcb-950d-4c28-a1c4-31ea4d744508}} of the anomalous chiral Lagrangian is here only to be used to explain our method. Ref.{{cite:6b930fed56923262cdf370343c8b60c7e7f3c383}} only expresses the Wess-Zumino-Witten term in terms of a parameter integration. In this section, we will explicitly finish this parameter integration and show that it does recover the Wess-Zumino-Witten term. Since we are only interested in the {{formula:7e0adb91-93dd-47bc-a539-a119a8cff16a}} field dependent part of the anomalous part of the chiral Lagrangian, we can drop out the pure source terms. Then our choice of {{formula:27ae6108-d253-403d-a833-51e7c37446ac}} in (REF ) gives the result that only {{formula:7ba5617b-753e-46ec-b078-c5c06256d904}} dependent terms in {{formula:85e2318b-c50f-4f41-9d9e-0809189a0602}} contribute to the chiral Lagrangian, while the {{formula:557bc4a7-49ee-4b15-a69c-2db080086e49}} independent terms in {{formula:e92263a7-a3b2-4a53-a6c6-a895afa2efc1}} are completely canceled by the term {{formula:270c8753-0ce2-4e62-857b-b1b59eb2563d}} in {{formula:82bd1c5c-74ed-45e1-80bb-fea298fe4e1a}} , leaving a pure {{formula:1d789a0d-4a9e-4ada-a69b-4ea7167f75cf}} field independent term {{formula:ea2e7cf8-286f-455f-ae52-5b4e78900e7a}} . heading: We summarize some drawbacks of random vertex and edge sampling:
section_text:
Random edge sampling may be impractical when edges cannot be randomly queried (e.g., online social networks like Facebook {{cite:bba33f242f24bb35c2d39da418a825c2d1cf4cfe}}, MySpace {{cite:d1a72d73d981d8a5ebf92ee4c73a951699277662}}, and Twitter or a P2P network like Bittorrent).

Random vertex sampling may be undesirable when user-ids are sparsely populated (low hit-to-miss ratio) and queries are subject to resource constraints (e.g., queries are rate-limited in Flickr, Livejournal {{cite:0d8a87541917c9e72b0c7edeaa29acd96454e376}}, and Bittorrent {{cite:c5b30c1f6092fb6ad4985aaa3db2ee3e7820ab49}}). In a P2P network like Bittorrent, a client can randomly sample peers (vertices) by querying a tracker (server); however, trackers may rate-limit client queries {{cite:c5b30c1f6092fb6ad4985aaa3db2ee3e7820ab49}}.

Even when random vertex sampling is not severely resource-constrained, some characteristics may be better estimated with random edge sampling (e.g., the tail of the degree distribution of a graph).

An alternative, and often cheaper, way to sample a network is by means of a random walk (RW).
A RW samples a graph by moving a particle (walker) from a vertex to a neighboring vertex (over an edge).
By this process edges and vertices are sampled.
The probability by which the random walker selects the next neighboring vertex determines the probability by which vertices and edges are sampled.
In this work we are interested in random walks that sample edges uniformly.
The edges sampled by RW can then be used to obtain unbiased estimates of a variety of graph characteristics (we present two examples in Section ).

In this work we assume that a random walker has the ability to query a vertex to obtain all of its incoming and outgoing edges (Section  details the reason behind this assumption).
This is possible for online networks such as Twitter, LiveJournal {{cite:0d8a87541917c9e72b0c7edeaa29acd96454e376}}, YouTube {{cite:0d8a87541917c9e72b0c7edeaa29acd96454e376}}, Facebook {{cite:bba33f242f24bb35c2d39da418a825c2d1cf4cfe}}, MySpace {{cite:d1a72d73d981d8a5ebf92ee4c73a951699277662}}, P2P networks {{cite:f02496846070308c8f494590d1d01543437abe1a}}, and the arXiv citations network.
We revisit the theory behind random walks in Section .

Sampling graphs with random walks is not without drawbacks.
The accuracy of the estimates depends not only on the graph structure but also on the characteristic being estimated.
The graph structure can create distortions in the estimates by “trapping” the random walker inside a subgraph.
An extreme case happens when the graph consists of two or more disconnected components (subgraphs).
For instance, wireless mobile social networks exhibit connection graphs with multiple disconnected components {{cite:950bee3bfb6bf6c0fe71c27fc328c9934cf1fc58}}.
But even connected graphs can suffer from the same problem.
A random walker can get “temporarily trapped” and spend most of its sampling budget exploring the local neighborhood near where it got “trapped”.
In the above scenarios estimates may be inaccurate if the characteristics of the local neighborhood differ from the overall characteristic of the graph.
This problem is well documented (see {{cite:64ea89968d026e758ebf4ae9dbe0abda87aa860b}}) and our goal is to mitigate it.

This work proposes a new {{formula:38a450f4-65d6-4408-879b-cb761405e558}} -dimensional random walk sampling method (Frontier sampling) that, starting from a collection of {{formula:981066b9-fc3c-4612-bafa-21c75d7c2a25}}  randomly sampled vertices, preserves all of the important statistical properties of a regular random walk (e.g., vertices are visited with a probability proportional to their degree).
While the vertices are visited with a probability proportional to their degree, we show that the joint steady state distribution of Frontier Sampling (the joint distribution of all {{formula:ce9fa204-8cd1-4d98-8068-fc40f7117b65}}  vertices) is closer to uniform (the starting distribution) than that of {{formula:dea9d728-b885-40ef-bffe-4373217576c5}}  independent random walkers, for any {{formula:a0c919af-cdcc-4970-839a-bd613013f3f8}} .
This property has the potential to dramatically reduce the transient of random walks.

In our simulations using real world graphs we see that Frontier Sampling mitigates the large estimation errors caused by disconnected or loosely connected components that can “trap” a random walker and distort the estimated graph characteristic, i.e., Frontier sampling (FS) estimates have smaller Mean Squared Errors (MSEs) than estimates obtained from regular random walkers (single and multiple independent walkers, reviewed in Section REF ) in a variety of scenarios.

We make two additional contributions: (1) we compare random walk-based estimates to those obtained from random vertex and random edge sampling. We show analytically that the tail of the degree distribution is better estimated using random edge sampling than random vertex sampling. We observe from simulations over real world networks (in Section REF ) that FS accuracy is comparable to the accuracy of random edge sampling. These results help explain recent empirical results {{cite:f02496846070308c8f494590d1d01543437abe1a}};
(2) we present asymptotically unbiased estimators using the edges sampled by a RW for the assortative mixing coefficient (defined in Section REF ) and the global clustering coefficient (defined in Section REF ).

The outline of this work is as follows.
Section  presents the notation used in this paper.
Section  contrasts random vertex with random edge sampling.
Section  revisits single and multiple independent random walk sampling and estimation.
Section  introduces Frontier Sampling (FS), a sampling process that uses {{formula:301d219e-e32b-4816-be32-1c163761b433}}  dependent random walkers in order to mitigate the high estimation errors caused by disconnected or loosely connected components.
Section  also shows that FS can be seen as an {{formula:2320c961-f5ef-4ed6-8d1a-01910ceab876}} -dimensional random walk over the {{formula:7748e697-8382-472b-96a0-2935fc51c4d8}} -th Cartesian power of the graph (formally defined in Section ).
In Section  we see that FS outperforms both single and multiple independent random walkers in a variety of scenarios.
We also compare (independent) random vertex and edge sampling with FS.
Section  reviews the relevant literature.
Finally, Section  presents our conclusions and future work.

In what follows we present some definitions.
Let {{formula:f31a55ac-0572-4b8c-a44d-6b3588cf54ba}}  be a labeled directed graph representing the (original) network graph, where {{formula:09adff2d-4988-4567-b8bb-e6b5e538b274}}  is a set of vertices and {{formula:b4c27c51-9a72-4cf6-aa0b-f578bdd949b9}}  is a set of ordered pairs of vertices {{formula:2dde9e61-076d-4c20-b991-7f22c19f19c4}}  representing a connection from {{formula:a03ece72-36c8-4bc1-9ffb-793b5b1f182d}}  to {{formula:dfed109e-22a7-4f68-ae4c-5280d2af56f3}}  (a.k.a. edges).
We assume that each vertex in {{formula:8ef5e078-c350-43b4-80d9-9a1b9eed7201}}  has at least one incoming or outgoing edge.

In this section we review random walk (RW) sampling and estimation over a non-bipartite, connected, directed, symmetric graph {{formula:8fcebb62-8e43-4ce6-9dd8-1c29180d5343}} .
Sampling {{formula:0d61a40f-7df2-4d13-a6cf-b5314d54b5fb}}  with a RW is straightforward.
The random walker has a sampling budget {{formula:a3ab42be-a3cf-410e-9c8b-2fc1d05fe27a}}  and starts at vertex {{formula:642b8f1d-64b5-4966-82ca-e572d7483454}} .
For the sake of simplicity, unless stated otherwise, we consider that all queries to vertices have unit cost and that we have a fixed sampling budget {{formula:d458243b-3d86-4f26-bd09-88d71303f514}} .

Let {{formula:2571735b-8bb0-41b7-b606-7303d72cb76b}}  be the a sequence of edges sampled by a RW, where {{formula:f9a28e9a-6636-4d14-b248-500da49dd098}} .
Note that edges may be sampled multiple times.
We refer to {{formula:2b504a5c-93d0-4f8a-88d8-c67643093e80}}  as the {{formula:44d1690f-c343-495e-8b23-b494f40b7b74}} -th sampled edge.
At the {{formula:40206e3e-b004-40ce-ab9f-59413bf3d285}} -th step a walker at vertex {{formula:fde47af3-9978-4917-a19a-cf9efdfbe06f}}  chooses an outgoing edge {{formula:9b2232d0-25f0-427c-8885-7dd6a79e264f}}  uniformly at random from the set of outgoing edges of {{formula:288b4255-caf4-4023-a01f-854c0e914e9b}}  and adds {{formula:8600f775-5f00-4504-a45f-bce4cd7ec57d}}  to the sequence of sampled edges.
At step {{formula:d6ca42d8-6a83-4870-9bab-945bab70fd8c}}  the random walker starts at vertex {{formula:4c535931-2fa4-482c-b546-07fff448d39a}}  and the sampling continues until {{formula:d8de9eee-24d2-4f0f-b9e8-c21b725a734f}} .

The RW described here is the most common type of RW found in the literature {{cite:a686af1c57eb9658c463e9cb5b2bedeaef9d27ea}}.
Other types of random walks differ in the way in which outgoing edges are sampled.
The Metropolis-Hastings RW {{cite:d4b6ff006046dc80e9d5aa3d57619eaaef2cc147}} is an example of a random walk that samples vertices (not edges) uniformly at random.
However, experiments estimating a variety of metrics indicate that Metropolis-Hastings RW is less accurate than the random walk described in this work {{cite:bba33f242f24bb35c2d39da418a825c2d1cf4cfe}}, {{cite:f02496846070308c8f494590d1d01543437abe1a}}.
For more details about other types of RW please refer to {{cite:e71430ab930af03df04a57af291baf84f45f1d08}}.

An important property of a RW is its ability to reach a unique stationary regime.
A necessary condition for stationarity is that {{formula:d4356a40-32df-40e9-a901-d4383fd2de62}}  must be symmetric, connected, and non-bipartite (the non-bipartite assumption can be relaxed in a lazy random walk {{cite:a686af1c57eb9658c463e9cb5b2bedeaef9d27ea}}).
In a stationary RW, the sequence of sampled edges is a stationary sequence.
A sequence {{formula:259aa6bc-f7f7-474b-ab7e-83ace15df2f0}}  of random variables is said to be stationary if for any positive integers {{formula:74393377-0d65-4d5d-b571-7b1a0962f53e}}  and {{formula:ecd93834-0531-4042-9c91-3eb7f9154c19}} , the joint distribution of {{formula:67ac51f8-3b79-444a-935b-676d4dfa80d9}}  is independent of {{formula:18304ea4-a8f0-4f5f-8c3d-a64d552d02a4}} .
Once the RW reaches steady state, it also shares two important properties with random edge (RE) sampling.
First, both RW and RE sample edges uniformly at random {{cite:a686af1c57eb9658c463e9cb5b2bedeaef9d27ea}}, which means that the probability that a vertex {{formula:1d66e66f-dada-412e-bd94-79ca76fa8aba}}  is sampled is {{formula:3e5d3b97-6d95-4149-baaa-34b7ac80fd57}} 
Second, both RW and RE obey the strong law of large numbers, as we see next.

The following variation of the strong law of large numbers is a powerful tool to build (asymptotically) unbiased estimators of graph characteristics.

section_text: limitations of the query framework. Moreover, the scripts, combining test input activity, telemetry gathering, and test evaluation, proved difficult to read — for other test engineers and for developers and systems engineers trying to extract and understand (and perhaps fix) a specification. Runtime verification using formal specifications offered a solution, and the MSL ground communications system suggested that we exploit an under-used approach to runtime verification: offline examination of event logs already produced by system execution. In the remainder of this paper we report on two aspects of this project — in Section we discuss the general idea of event sequences as requirements, and our specification methodology; Section gives a brief introduction to our application of these general ideas to MSL and our new specification language. Systems verification consists of proving that an artifact (hardware and/or software) satisfies a specification. In mathematical terms we have a model {{formula:3b79aeaf-4188-4ac6-a7f0-eee1c91d1222}} (for example the complete system) in some model language {{formula:bbadcbc0-a22b-477c-9ef8-cfffa303793b}} , and a specification {{formula:124a3111-f125-4993-994f-6732fd0610c4}} in some specification language {{formula:a513cd2f-f905-4ff6-b1ce-56bc94be3ea6}} , and we want to show that the pair {{formula:2735e822-6276-4751-82e0-c1b3b58916e2}} is member of the satisfaction relation {{formula:a88ebbec-0138-4e3d-aa62-ef95b37352bf}} , also typically written: {{formula:472b43b1-82d1-4bba-94e6-27ad72b07d1e}} . The general problem of demonstrating correctness of a combined hardware/software system is very hard, as is well-known. Advanced techniques such as theorem proving or model checking tend not to scale for practical purposes. Extracting abstract models of the system, and proving these correct, has been shown to sometimes be useful, but also faces scalability problems when dealing with real systems or complex properties. The problem is inherently difficult because the models are complex – because the behavior of systems is complex. The problems of full verification have long limited the adoption of formal specification. In runtime verification a specification is used to analyze a single execution of a system, not the complete behavior. In this case a model is a single execution trace {{formula:8a4a4730-5a6e-4968-8ec4-9e4ea4931f9c}} , and the verification problem consists of demonstrating that {{formula:b87c9ce3-3fa2-44fb-814f-e0fe1848c180}} , a much simpler problem with scalable solutions. The original model {{formula:b2658737-8dd6-4faa-ae8e-53f0832d82df}} (the full system) can be considered as denoting the set of all possible runs {{formula:6261cf80-68ef-4b6e-b494-0dcef8df94f1}} , of which we now only verify a subset. This approach of course is less ambitious, but seems to be a practical and useful deployment of formal specification. Though these observations are well known, they are less often taken into practice. It is still rare to observe the application of formal specification — even for runtime verification. There may be several reasons for this, one of which is the problem of program instrumentation. A large body of research considers the problem: how to we produce traces to verify? There is, however, a much simpler approach, namely to use logging information that is already generated by almost any computer system when it is tested. Our first recommendation is therefore that runtime verification should be used to formally check logged data. Our second recommendation is that logging and requirements engineering should be connected in the sense that requirements should be testable through runtime verification of logs. The common element is the event: requirements should be expressed as predicates on sequences of events, and logging should produce such sequences of events, thereby making the requirements testable. This means that logs preferably should consist of events with a formal template, connected to the original requirements. Note, however, that it is possible to extract formalized events from chaotic logging information produced by the usual ad hoc methods — using, e.g., regular expressions. The obvious scientific and methodological question is: what kind of information should a log contain, in order to help verify requirements? We shall adopt the simple view that a log is a sequence of events, where an event is a mapping from names to values of various types (integers, strings, etc.): {{formula:fdc81f6a-89f6-4ffa-a9fa-16cc01ab85c2}} This definition is quite general. An event can carry information about various aspects of the observed system. Events can be classified into various kinds by letting a designated name, i.e. kind, map to the kind. In the context of MSL, five forms of events are used, see Figure REF . We claim that these five event kinds are generally applicable to any system being monitored. The five forms of events are: (1) commands (input) issued to the monitored system, (2) products (output) delivered by the system, (3) periodic samplings of the state of the system, such as the value of continuous-valued sensors (like position coordinates), (4) changes to the state of the system, those changes that are observable, and (5) transitions performed by the system (also referred to as EVent Reports - EVRs), for example when printf statements would normally be used to record an important event. The two forms of observation of the state (3, 4) could potentially be regarded as one kind of observation: that of the state of the system at any point in time. The state observations (3, 4) and the transitions (5) are internal events, while the commands (1) and products (2) are external events. {{figure:4ca9135c-c50c-4e7c-84f1-8031b1eb060a}} We have developed a specification language, and corresponding monitoring system, to be presented in the next section, which have been applied by testing engineers within the MSL project. The specification language consists of a mixture of automata and temporal logic with elements of regular expressions. The logic can specifically refer to the data in events. This mixture seems to be attractive for the engineers. In the longer term,

Thus (REF ) follows. Second part. We will do the case {{formula:04d84dc0-c67d-4bde-8458-cb9727d7ab0b}} ; the others are analogous. The set of vertexes of {{formula:e2df6dea-c2f6-48fe-9f11-221d9a745ea6}} is disjoint union {{formula:d7db96d3-9d97-46b3-9851-e521fae879bd}} , where {{formula:b2aa5e6c-1c53-4b19-8c3b-88910817261d}} denotes the set of vertexes of {{formula:a9768214-c2b1-4625-b123-60f6531f0e26}} . We connect two vertexes {{formula:87708674-596b-4567-b3c8-3a758b131afc}} and {{formula:f5888715-e302-4175-8875-864f50eb2a9a}} iff the pairs {{formula:c3d85f7b-3cbf-4b8e-8a61-4aaa7bb266e1}} and {{formula:0e1d6cf2-db5f-456c-93ea-4387871c3c7d}} were connected in {{formula:92a48391-51f1-4591-a33d-744e1fc65122}} ; the length of this edge must be maximum of lengths of edges {{formula:a06dae46-95e7-4235-ad11-caa6dbe2cafa}} and {{formula:5d4263bd-e2ea-46b4-9b3f-5cdc726b5de2}} (we assume that a vertex is connected to it-self by an edge of length 0). Clearly, there is a homeomorphism {{formula:1583460e-e70d-479b-af3b-0a91a580bbd2}} . Note that there are two short coordinate projections {{formula:a6299013-280f-47ca-9910-2054778b8bbe}} . Thus for any path {{formula:a342f15e-6164-4948-9949-e37c72d28da3}} , we have that total length of {{formula:59b73409-ed8e-4f4c-8fe3-72cd97a13de3}} is at least as big as {{formula:0449bd76-bdb1-4155-9d17-6d2b535a6be7}} . That ensures that pulled back metric on {{formula:81a76fc3-5a3b-4aa1-b62f-7740cdf29486}} is bi-Lipschitz to the product metric on {{formula:d7d5962e-c6bf-40ac-b232-89ed55d9f615}} . {{formula:752f165d-ffb8-4856-9620-99c6ca4faee5}} A length space {{formula:a4544ead-defb-4276-b765-40e76c6999ec}} is called Minkowski {{formula:77078e72-5fa9-44a4-a7d2-f970bdf49541}} -polyhedron if there is a finite triangulation of {{formula:a36a1115-64bc-478c-aca2-f0d49ec1a336}} such that each simplex is isometric to a simplex in a Minkowski space. Correspondingly, a compact metric space {{formula:79ce648b-e748-41ec-9cae-9f6507423698}} is called pro-Minkowski space of rank {{formula:07bec19e-69e8-4b40-99d2-87f507ce0fd6}} if it can be presented as an inverse limit of Minkowski {{formula:8a5d7026-f74d-40eb-9de5-11050b7b578e}} -polyhedra. 5.1. Question. Is it true that any length space with Lebesgue's covering dimension {{formula:774b5313-06de-44a1-95f2-beaed0e251d2}} is a pro-Minkowski space of rank {{formula:b16bb62b-bd38-4810-87d2-630903c31f67}} ? Or even more specific: 5.2. Question. Is it true that any metric space which homeomorphic to a disk is a pro-Minkowski space of rank 2? One can reformulate it philosophically: Is there any essential difference between Finsler metric and general metric on {{formula:4b196835-86ff-4111-aac0-2b306888230d}} -manifold? This question was asked by D. Burago; it was also original motivation for this paper (see also a related example {{cite:4b3a40a9723f5f4c1782eb66258c556b4393109b}}). If one removes restriction on dimension, then the answer to the above question is YES. Namely, the following exercise can be solved by using Kuratowski embedding {{formula:bb9d555e-da50-497a-9f3a-b9570f7110d0}} . 5.3. Exercise. Show that any compact length space is an inverse limit of Minkowski polyhedra {{formula:90e1f384-4762-47a6-99c2-f08df22dbe88}} with {{formula:3387e88b-1694-4352-b033-a53e31cc1187}} . 5.4. Question. Is it true that any path isometry from a closed Euclidean ball to Euclidean space is an intrinsic isometry?

section_text: future work directions. In this section, we first introduce the real trading data from the Shanghai Futures Exchange, which will be used for constructing futures trading networks, and then present the details of the construction of futures trading networks. For constructing the futures trading networks, we use real trading records from the Shanghai Futures Exchange, which is the largest one in China's domestic futures market and has considerable impact on the global derivative market. Trade records are generated by matching orders or quotes from buyers and sellers according to a certain rule of price/time priority (first price, then time) via the electronic trading platform of the futures exchange. There are hundreds of thousands of matching results reported from the exchange in one typical trading day. We use a dataset involving all futures commodities in the derivative market from July to September, 2008. For the trading records, we use virtual and unique IDs for representing the trading participants, and all other sensitive information is filtered for privacy preservation reason. Since a trading record contains the IDs of both the buyer and the seller, we are able to establish a futures trading network. The construction process is as follows. A node represents a participant in a trading record, and an edge, meaning a trade relation, is established between two participants if their IDs appear simultaneously at least once in one trading record. An example of FTN that comprises nine records is shown in fig:example-ftn. Here, A-H are IDs of trading participants. Each row in the right table of fig:example-ftn represents a trading record where the seller and buyer columns are the IDs of seller and buyer. {{figure:41bbd92a-6fc7-4d9d-b105-48f7042c2d27}} Following the above process, we first create the largest network with the whole dataset containing three months' trading records; this network is denoted as FTN-all. Then, we construct three sub-networks based on three subsets of the whole dataset above according to the futures commodity classification of the Shanghai Futures Exchange. These three sub-networks are termed as FTN-met, FTN-rub and FTN-oil, which involve only futures commodity metal (concretely including copper, aluminum, zinc and gold), natural rubber and fuel oil, respectively. Thus, we have totally four FTNs, their statistic information is given in tab:ftns. {{table:ef05c406-1eee-428a-9be5-f983b2d41fc5}} In what follows, we study the characteristics of FTNs constructed above, our focus is on topological features and dynamical properties. Extensive empirical results are presented. The degree distribution P(k) is one of the most important statistical characteristics of a network, and also one of the simplest properties that can be measured directly. It is defined as the probability that a random node in a network has exactly k edges. In many real complex networks, P(k) decays with {{formula:2356863c-0813-48b9-b2b9-31dd089ec935}} in a power law, following {{formula:cce3dbe2-644d-4a89-a809-82e0cb8b2110}} A network that owns such a property is called a scale-free network {{cite:5156cf27f63ef5540ba06955bd4e5e8bf58771ea}}. We plot the degree distributions {{formula:f2eaf395-8108-43a1-b055-8642aa783165}} of FTN-all, FTN-met, FTN-rub and FTN-oil in fig:degree-distribution(a)-(d). Our observation of the subplots implies that all the four FTNs are scale-free networks. However, reaching a conclusion that all FTNs are scale-free requires a deeper analysis by statistic techniques. {{figure:6fa1b423-5976-415d-846d-5768071123bb}} To detect the existence of power-law property in FTNs, we consider the cumulative degree distribution function defined as {{formula:b291a9e4-72f5-4840-b61b-3b280f71a328}} because the power-law cumulative degree distribution of a network means that its degree distribution obeys a power law {{cite:88c867e493717d99764eb64b9838374f0d06e77c}}. According to Ref. {{cite:ebb16d5e1c2a73543d7dc318c2362c82ad0b6351}}, we calculate the complementary cumulative degree distributions of FTNs for estimating the scaling parameter {{formula:1684a224-4108-40d6-a46d-d3016aa281bf}} and the lower bound {{formula:48131fdf-08eb-4bd8-9a38-72537f086922}} of power-law behavior based on the methods of maximum likelihood estimators and the quantification of the distance between two probability distributions. Furthermore, we conduct a goodness-of-fit test by computing the distance between the empirical distribution of FTN and the power-law model with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) statistic, and generating a p-value that quantifies the plausibility of a power-law degree distribution hypothesis for each FTN. The cumulative degree distributions {{formula:4c814feb-79a3-4dd0-86b5-a60a139e7707}} for all the four networks are presented in fig:cumulative-degree-distribution with the slope ({{formula:5ef9ceae-387f-4bf9-a48d-29b51235a69e}} -1). tab:dd-fit-test gives the estimations of {{formula:d9698a78-b5ef-4d1c-863d-a96cdf58c498}} , {{formula:f74188fa-fdb5-47c6-bcf2-72e1fcbb44f3}} , and the p-value of the goodness-of-fit test for each power-law fit of FTN. {{figure:e81cc8c7-f57c-4c98-ac2b-2f3be4197161}}{{table:12ce23e9-f01b-4f62-a0ed-c7acf2031b4c}} As listed in tab:dd-fit-test, the scaling parameters {{formula:2794bd20-4d46-40db-9427-cb5f52d1bd60}} of the four FTNs have nearly similar values of 2.48, 2.39, 2.53 and 2.39 for FTN-all, FTN-met, FTN-run and FTN-oil, respectively. Their p-values are 0.225, 0.106, 0.591 and 0.674, respectively, which provide sufficient evidence indicating that the power law is a plausible hypothesis for the degree distribution of each FTN. These results imply that highly connected nodes have larger possibilities of happening and dominating the connectivity of FTNs. Actually, these nodes correspond to a few active speculators who issue numerous orders to the exchange, and consequently have more opportunities to make deals with the others. Their trading behaviors also account for the fact that FTNs dynamically expand in accordance with the rule of preferential attachment by continuously adding new nodes during the lifetime of a network. In fig:degree-distribution, we can also see the fact that in low-degree regions, the probability of even degree (say {{formula:27c27375-0b1e-445f-8a47-ca5398c28703}} =2{{formula:119318c8-dbf0-4458-856d-4e3dc02ab990}} ) is larger than that of odd degree ({{formula:6cb4a6fb-ac9d-4d51-957d-c0eea34f5931}} =2{{formula:b316a3fd-7577-4fc2-987e-2e22c03a7ddd}} +1), which forms a divergence. As the degree increases, the two branches gradually reach to a convergence and the difference is averaged out. The branch of even degree conforms to power law more than that of the odd one. One reasonable explanation on this observation is that most participants of low degree, entering the futures market as speculators, cautiously

section_text: future research directions. For readers interested in their own implementation, we note that some details regarding the multiscale scheme (that are not related strongly to the discussed problem) are omitted in this paper; they can be found in {{cite:ef209d77302c2b6c2da3d855c9c327c94c66534d}}, {{cite:3cd785597de45df3eba7365459f429ef7f1ae34e}}, {{cite:56a3f0fdbdf1ad82427383150a56050f879c591b}}, {{cite:d4d583f6bb4759e40de854328c25508c38742fcb}}. A network is described by a weighted directed graph {{formula:cd405517-26d3-464d-9095-1db667e4bb0e}} , where {{formula:53033c34-6e25-4fdc-9e4f-e417b0bdb6c5}} is the set of nodes (vertices) and {{formula:0f6e05cf-170b-4be2-b3a5-baec10d06ee7}} is the set of directed edges. If {{formula:e11bbe92-2b09-4aa5-850b-025caab38a8b}} , then there exists an edge {{formula:e5d31f19-6a43-439b-9f8e-02c80dd33f21}} . Denote by {{formula:3e7d101a-902b-4d11-8a3c-bf72287ab1f0}} the non-negative weight of the directed edge {{formula:08081336-2f87-40b8-bb68-11adf7107bd4}} between nodes {{formula:3d0899a9-c5a8-4c18-b94c-705c5ae1ac7d}} and {{formula:7dd306ad-fa3f-4a69-86e1-b185c7108c7a}} ; if {{formula:b16f9c72-9f70-4331-99de-ec594c3565cf}} , then {{formula:5a8863f0-35af-4866-b9ef-f71055ed9fde}} . Let {{formula:b8e5947c-9ad7-4a6f-8fa1-9f110fd2e700}} be a bijection {{formula:180c5ee8-ee27-49c3-b51f-d105f1a3fef4}} The purpose of the link-weighted version of the minimum logarithmic arrangement problem (MLogA) is to minimize {{formula:ee822e3e-86eb-4152-85c2-67bc5afc993b}} over all possible permutations {{formula:4cc213df-183d-49ce-8704-ff35e8fd6793}} . The base of a logarithm ({{formula:85f7c9d6-dcc2-41ec-b479-c3bf6f786781}} ) will be always 2. We define the generalized form of this problem (GMLogA) that emerges during the multilevel solver; each vertex {{formula:af97c83e-a6d0-46bd-881a-dfb95a1a4611}} is assigned with a {{formula:e1854c4b-22ce-4bbe-ba55-9786f5d51af0}} (or {{formula:7490ac23-bd86-40a3-8f9a-b705510ed564}} ), denoted {{formula:773d6af5-57c3-4930-acdc-42e28666ac49}} . Given the vector of all volumes, {{formula:a5d53c7a-3bc2-4cab-90dd-29efa64a087f}} , the task now is to minimize the cost {{formula:e8c47be3-83ac-4a07-8a6c-cb47c880465e}} over all possible {{formula:75795a40-f4e2-4357-9c60-d2dcee183529}} , where {{formula:66f37f8f-0a91-4729-abf1-5791aef5e4a9}}; that is, each vertex is positioned at its center of mass, capturing a segment on the real axis that equals its length. The original form of the problem is the special case where all the volumes are equal. We denote the process of creating a weighted undirected graph {{formula:4fff2dcc-2d6e-4b95-94cf-c91ba046f9a8}} by {{formula:25df6efb-f34e-4b9f-ad41-4526642845bb}} , where {{formula:498cc733-f9e1-4879-85a3-6c611ac0c1f1}} is a given directed graph. By applying {{formula:2bc742cb-86e7-4315-ae60-f59020f46185}} , we obtain {{formula:f6b2d079-7b8f-4b65-835f-157232fec703}} and {{formula:98eafc1b-3c75-44a2-b989-6642628191f8}} The edge weights are accumulated from the set of directed edges {{formula:f7b43470-5973-4ce2-8dff-26e649abb47b}} allowing use of multigraphs. Both MLogA and GMLogA are formulated for the undirected graphs similarly to their directed versions. In this paper we will find approximate solutions for the following problem: Problem 2.1 Given a directed weighted network graph {{formula:a295846e-696f-4877-b0e4-df11c72d0362}} , the objective is to find a permutation {{formula:5f808a1e-0f89-439f-bebe-ec3a8d0eebf8}} that minimizes {{formula:92b7a888-c177-4753-9e7a-7ace1c31c096}} , where {{formula:281d998f-5b3d-4e7c-a9b5-90bf9282d326}} is a vector of the respective node coordinates restricted by {{formula:0f67875a-2a33-4224-bbe2-df81dcd089f5}} . Note that the problem is formulated for both directed and undirected graphs. We define{{formula:0adda824-d2fc-4cb3-ab9b-732856fd2f43}} with no subindexes will be used where appropriate. {{formula:3600a5cb-2905-4809-a190-ec71a5440ceb}} as the main unit for the empirical comparison in Section : {{formula:7516c7f2-bfcc-4f71-9aeb-dcbe0cf46fcb}} In the multiscale framework we construct a hierarchy of decreasing-size graphs, {{formula:b82a61a3-ef0e-4a79-a2b3-eaefc19e517e}} , by coarsening, starting from the given graph {{formula:a6bc0324-bbf4-497e-9db6-5211db045511}} . In other words, we create an undirected version of a given directed graph by assigning to the undirected edges bigger weights if, in the original unweighted graph, the directed edges had been reciprocal. At the coarsest level Problem REF is solved exactly, and starting from the {{formula:b0da62bf-4b24-423a-bf67-f92a7e21a63f}} th level it is formulated and approximated by successive prolongation of the solution from the previous coarser level. This entire process is called a {{formula:b49e8cd0-5bb8-4d4a-95d8-83e14b2ff765}} -{{formula:5d5b57bd-5f41-4172-9bde-2badf76fa405}} (see Figure REF ). {{figure:a5fdaba6-29b6-4f21-92ff-09b12f96f91e}} In the present work, coarsening is interpreted as a modified process of weighted aggregation reinforced by the algebraic distance couplings for logarithmic sum minimization. For a detailed discussion about the algebraic distance-based weighted aggregation and multiscale graph organization related to the general graph optimization problems, we refer the reader to {{cite:56a3f0fdbdf1ad82427383150a56050f879c591b}}. We will briefly repeat its basic components for the completeness of the paper and will concentrate on the modifications related to Problem REF . Algebraic distance-based coupling is a measure of connectivity strength between two nodes connected by an edge {{cite:56a3f0fdbdf1ad82427383150a56050f879c591b}}, {{cite:7891df83cba7627f89ae18bf190420cbd6e5545d}}. Given the Laplacian of a graph, denoted by {{formula:fa93eece-2465-4354-88d5-bd9321cf4b9d}} , where {{formula:d5c6a5c8-2d3e-4bf3-9278-a3ab943a4f11}} is a weighted adjacency matrix of a graph and {{formula:80c8ec82-91e3-4330-bb34-9859c4bf7c45}} is the diagonal matrix with entries {{formula:a8a9e155-59b7-478e-9dc6-a32763e074a0}} , we define an iteration matrix {{formula:54a3bc5b-a546-4d35-b598-392bddc46550}} for Jacobi over-relaxation (JOR) as {{formula:e2f473ea-a7a3-4228-923d-1dc050a3bf68}} where {{formula:a8dba4f9-65dc-473e-9b40-884e6c339776}} (see Appendix A) and {{formula:8dc370c6-6c66-43da-b180-df0ccfa348cc}} and {{formula:70ccab2d-7c35-4b94-a88e-1dba5c4a6439}} are the strict lower and upper triangular parts of {{formula:7f5a7ac6-96c1-4301-a83c-ad48f2e2ccaa}} , respectively. Definition 3.1 The algebraic distance coupling {{formula:51304845-b836-49f4-96b9-10f8fca9d93d}} is defined as {{formula:768ba19b-9025-4646-b398-b98dbfa72c07}} where {{formula:b4a85656-72e8-4a9f-98d4-864e6177c640}} is a relaxed randomly initialized test vector (i.e., {{formula:099a190d-23d5-4444-9d13-ee7b40f72c02}} is a random vector sampled over [-1/2, 1/2]), R is a number of initial test vectors, and k is a number of iterations. Note that this definition is a modified version of the original definition from {{cite:56a3f0fdbdf1ad82427383150a56050f879c591b}}, {{cite:7891df83cba7627f89ae18bf190420cbd6e5545d}} which makes it more suitable for Problem REF . Several interesting properties (including convergence and model description) still can be proved similarly to {{cite:7891df83cba7627f89ae18bf190420cbd6e5545d}}. Considering {{formula:c016ee5d-1e0f-41f0-b74d-a357d1b5ce1d}} as an edge strength measure, one can construct a coarse graph by defining a classical AMG interpolation matrix {{formula:ec7288d1-12b2-4a12-9ee2-46e63b66f2c8}} that will project the fine graph to the coarse graph (i.e., to the lower-dimensional space). The projection is represented as {{formula:49392c39-c2cd-4754-adb3-4722d8554dcd}} where {{formula:4985a9f5-2a16-4f8e-85d1-4b75c14c0b16}} and {{formula:8149489a-a653-4853-a8b4-6088834bd8d9}} are the Laplacians of fine ({{formula:470acad8-2acc-48dc-8216-e85380b028ed}} ) and coarse ({{formula:a33789a5-cc19-4755-92e0-9d136e58bfb2}} ) graphs, respectively. We begin by selecting a set of seed nodes {{formula:c54af1db-c71b-4913-b285-6c242768c5c3}} that will represent the centers of future coarse nodes (or aggregates). In this paper, we present non-LTM mass models which perfectlyWhile the observed image positions do have (small) observational uncertainties of a pixel ({{formula:a07bacc0-bbed-463a-a064-7f34be5a49ac}} ) or so, our solutions do perfectly fit the data as input. reproduce the observed (lensed) input positions of 168 multiple images of 55 knots residing within 135 images of 42 galaxies. The resolution of a reconstructed mass model is given roughly by the spatial density of the multiple image constraints , . Thus our model which incorporates 135 multiple images has {{formula:59b02526-d055-4a97-8545-9130bf3fea34}} greater spatial resolution ({{formula:d683ff0c-d8a2-4f5d-bd92-cadebbee4c3b}} greater along each axis) than the aforementioned models which incorporate only {{formula:3a4b9d4c-0629-4b7e-bb32-101aab22f004}} multiple images. Our SL analysis method was made possible just recently thanks to the development of mathematical tools enabling one to obtain curl-free interpolations of a vector field which perfectly reproduce the input data at the input positions , . We make only minimal assumptions about the physicality of the mass distribution, including no assumptions about LTM. As the strongest known gravitational lens on our sky for some time, A1689 has provided us with an excellent laboratory. It was the first cluster to have its mass measured via both analyses of weak lensing and magnification of the background galaxy population . Yet before A1689 was observed with ACS, no multiple images had been identified in the field except for two fold arcs, our 8ab and 13abc . These arcs were sufficient for a rudimentary strong lensing analysis to be performed yielding an Einstein radius of {{formula:a36e4325-2cd9-4398-98c4-627a6f1e04d5}} , the largest of any known lens at the time. With such a large Einstein radius, the ACS GTO team devoted 20 orbits to imaging the cluster, confident that it would reveal many highly magnified background galaxies and multiple image systems. The observations (obtained in 2002 June) delivered, and the 100+ multiple images still far surpass any other gravitational lens. To date, other clusters observed to the same depth have yielded far fewer multiple images: 53, 35, and 33 from A1703, A2218, and CL0024, respectively , , . Concentrations assuming an overdensity of 200 (converted from quoted values if necessary). b SL = strong lensing; WL = weak lensing; RE = Einstein radius; counts = magnification depletion; X-ray; dynamical = cluster galaxy velocity measurements c 3-{{formula:c96bd504-1b84-4872-a0a2-74209e5942b5}} uncertainties d Includes uncertainties due to halo triaxiality e Fit to ellipsoidal gNFW profile (with variable central slope) One result that stands out from both lensing and X-ray analyses of A1689 is that its mass appears to be more centrally concentrated than predicted by CDM simulations of structure formation. Simulated dark matter halos have mass profiles which are generally well described by NFW or Einasto / Sérsic profiles . More massive clusters (such as A1689) finished forming later when the universe was less dense overall, and thus are found (at least in simulations) to be less centrally concentrated. Yet where A1689 is expected to have a NFW concentration of {{formula:de72af7e-236f-4296-97eb-25d853803a1f}} ({{formula:d59d1566-3a2a-450b-aea3-13535419a546}} ), it has been shown observationally (Table ) to have a much higher concentration {{formula:e14886d6-e348-4f83-bb6a-5dda49be4d8a}} ({{formula:a9ce9cb8-bf86-4100-ba0f-0e0835025e94}} ) claim to account for A1689's high concentration (along with the discrepancy between lensing and X-ray masses) by fitting an 3-D ellipsoidal gNFW profile (with variable central slope) simultaneously to the SL, WL, and X-ray data. While the method is impressive, simulated clusters have yet to be analyzed in the same way (they are normally fit to spherical NFW profiles), so it is unclear that a direct comparison can be made.. As one of the strongest lenses on our sky, we might expect A1689's concentration to be on the high side. However, even accounting for triaxiality , and selection (lensing) bias , , , A1689's high concentration still seems extremely unlikely . Lensing analyses of larger samples of clusters seem to support the idea that clusters may have higher concentrations , , and larger Einstein radii , , than simulated clusters. However only a small lensing-biased sample of these have been studied in sufficient detail. We note that joint SL+WL fitting is required to constrain mass profiles well and concentrations to {{formula:c1e9f4c9-a034-4759-a7cc-6472026c08c6}} according to simulations . The addition of X-ray, SZ, and/or velocity dispersion data can constrain the mass profiles further still , , . section_text: future work and relate the approach to current work on XML query languages and XML database systems. This section briefly introduces the unified region/language model. The definitions closely follow Burkowski's model {{cite:ce0e7867c24f1d5eb7acd3df5148f3325873a46d}}, which we extend with region scores similar to the score region algebra we used for XML information retrieval {{cite:3de4821b1f4fe2dc701812fa4bec7990c289e1e6}}. A textual database consists of a finite sequence of words {{formula:50c31235-7fc8-44b3-8ff8-f0f6e6749801}} , where {{formula:bf306596-d543-4a70-85bf-ac9e7e23ad31}} is used to denote the word on position {{formula:a766220f-5d6a-460e-a038-26deec44ca6a}} in the database. Additionally, the textual database consists of a hierarchy of text elements. Both words and elements are identified by the word positions in the database. Text elements are sequences of words that have a particular significance in the database. For example, a database with recipes will have text elements “ingredients”, “quantities”, “instructions”, etc., typically marked up as XML. A scored region {{formula:16cd9d8d-c6eb-49c8-911a-41f959f18d23}} is defined by two integers {{formula:99e0a0cf-12ee-47cd-9074-d1533701abbf}} and {{formula:07235c02-4cc0-4644-a4c2-2dd8b3027d4e}} ({{formula:e3a9c750-5ccb-4014-84db-b129b09b75a6}} ), and a float {{formula:ba9245ae-e495-41b7-b90f-aab15bf16143}} ({{formula:d8c08790-6f2d-4a14-b1ec-7ac578e1313d}} ).We intentionally use a notation that is close to that of the relational data model; see also Figure REF . The integers start and end represent respectively the position of the first word that belongs to the contiguous region, and the position directly following the last word that belongs to the region. A region might be a text element, but also any other contiguous sequence of words. Note that the region {{formula:cfb5ffa2-7876-489a-9ccd-d1b0504cdb0f}} includes one (and only one) word {{formula:9f2605ac-fded-4718-82bc-5c13dad5a888}} with a score {{formula:3c55019f-e6bb-4fcc-b627-cf89c141ccf5}} . Retrieval from the textual database is done with a simple query language consisting of words, elements and five basic operators: CONTAINING, CONTAINED_BY, SCALE, AND, and OR. The language defines an algebra on sets of scored regions. Unlike Burkowski's model {{cite:ce0e7867c24f1d5eb7acd3df5148f3325873a46d}}, there are no additional constraints on sets of regions. We will now one-by-one define the language primitives in a rather informal way. For convenience, Figure REF contains a more formal definition of the operators using SQL. A word A single word, for example the query banana, produces a set of regions {{formula:911faa83-b7a0-4bdc-9148-8fa3dcf8e573}} , where each region {{formula:ad1d517f-37a0-47e9-9bf8-caba2f3d6434}} defines a position of the word in the textual database; {{formula:936b96b5-49ee-4f6f-8a2e-e6eb4850b409}} being the position on which the word occurs, {{formula:158bda82-b5b2-433f-9781-b2d23527b0bd}} , and {{formula:bf5b1971-90f8-4370-9825-267ff3ae99c7}} . An element A single element, for instance the query <recipe> produces a set of regions {{formula:ab0b7154-d38e-4649-8c49-ffdd79b1b1d6}} , where each region {{formula:2e1171b7-e970-493e-862b-15d9c3fa46fa}} is tagged as “recipe”, {{formula:cc5a8b22-1b8e-4180-bdc5-3fc50b366edc}} being the position of the first word of the XML element, {{formula:0b5fac00-633f-4687-af7f-188ce8adb56d}} being the position following the last word of the XML element, and {{formula:6f71c287-96f5-4d7d-b000-16b49d308b60}} . {{formula:f235fa01-3ef8-4ec7-afed-8e94a75d6fcd}} CONTAINING {{formula:239f7355-132f-48d4-848b-9f23ef0954eb}} The operator CONTAINING takes two sets of regions {{formula:d5ef5511-13c1-4a1b-a805-0fdfb9ceebd8}} and {{formula:436dfd48-59e6-437c-a1ec-7dd01b79029d}} , and produces the subset of regions from {{formula:e43c4fbd-2a24-4621-a4da-b6e6d305a57c}} that contain at least one region from {{formula:cb41c4cf-468b-4b7a-9117-2366bc580898}} . For instance, the query <recipe> CONTAINING banana produces all regions tagged as “recipe” that contain at least one occurrence of “banana”. Inspired by language models, each “recipe” region is scored by the number of occurrences of “banana” in the region, divided by the length of the region (measured as {{formula:477dc861-649b-47fc-8869-a904274d6212}} ). Occurrences of “banana” are weighted by their length and by their score (of course, in the example query both length = 1 as well as score = 1); see Figure REF . {{formula:1f7e69a2-1250-4ae7-ab6f-62fb570edfc2}}CONTAINED_BY{{formula:c01a13fb-f750-461d-9efd-65b5a1d30750}} The operator CONTAINED_BY takes two sets of regions {{formula:2ac00df1-0591-4c1b-b0a1-c76993e6d897}} and {{formula:d2adfc30-71a1-45f9-8549-d3c2aea17da1}} , and produces the subset of regions from {{formula:ed0ad2cd-af4b-4c12-b12a-6777f8de8b46}} that are at least contained by one region from {{formula:06069a8a-8d8a-458e-8896-48f4a5e0212b}} . For instance, the query <ingredient> CONTAINED_BY <recipe> produces all ingredients that belong at least to one recipe. If a region from the left-hand side of the expression is nested in more than one region from the right-hand side of the expression, then the scores of those regions are added. This will be used in the next section to express the linear combination of several language models; see Figure REF . {{formula:9144b60d-860e-44fe-998d-8ff6d76adeec}} SCALE {{formula:d1f92595-9ed0-4a6f-9326-3319c14b7a5a}} The operator SCALE takes a float {{formula:0fd6ba90-2293-49d1-beb6-ce89db653883}} and a set of regions {{formula:5d9d3369-0e86-4a52-b59d-7c0d723a9870}} and produces all regions from {{formula:3b991146-0124-4dc6-a537-44ccb3f33a4a}} where each region {{formula:b2a07e43-9db8-4da7-a02c-ca5304473f63}} is scored as {{formula:8af5d9e7-a86a-4656-b62f-c0fb74546b00}} . For instance, the query 0.2 SCALE banana produces the set of regions with the positions of the word “banana” all with a region score of 0.2; see Figure REF . {{formula:39f3a47e-9f34-4e3a-b6e3-87575f7033df}} AND {{formula:c936042e-8ee1-4d4c-9828-aca0ba640ce1}} The operator AND takes two sets of regions {{formula:f61d56a8-ae08-40ae-8338-cec84b444a49}} and {{formula:88c0551d-b90e-4118-ba90-24f33d1a0e11}} , and produces only those regions that are both in {{formula:febf9ed3-0002-40a6-b4ba-bd6d59bb8d84}} and {{formula:8886381f-6446-4d6a-b627-0ddfe2c5dc04}} , i.e., the intersection of both sets when ignoring the region scores. Each region in the result is scored by multiplying its scores in {{formula:6025b8d6-d189-403b-a31b-ae3ff50e7eed}} and {{formula:12320e0b-f1b2-4d56-a261-daf688e20415}} . For instance, the query (<recipe> CONTAINING banana) AND (<recipe> CONTAINING apple) produces all regions tagged as “recipe” that contain both the word “banana” and the word “apple”, scored by the product of the scores of the respective regions; see Figure REF . {{formula:9d257f68-8ffb-4586-9afc-c4c40b0a1ac8}} OR {{formula:8d2d6c7e-ad05-4728-9ba9-e577b905e763}} The operator OR takes two sets of regions {{formula:c11540e6-8044-4bab-ad83-f48aa2f2941f}} and {{formula:8ea3e604-42d7-4e09-bfb1-fb078cfcc52e}} , and produces those regions that either are in {{formula:8979dd09-ec25-4602-9130-8bd291c807f9}} , or in {{formula:2adb164e-29e3-4c1e-b091-22556b74c4cf}} , i.e., the union of both sets when ignoring the region scores. For instance, the query (<recipe> CONTAINING sugar){{formula:2aa116ee-f6c9-4fa9-a6ef-f5c254495fdd}}OR{{formula:a4bcff0a-9233-4e27-8c44-2846551e548b}} (<recipe> CONTAINING sweet) produces all regions tagged as “recipe” that contain either the word “sugar” or the word “sweet” (or both). Regions keep their score, unless both sets contain the region, in which case the region is scored by adding its scores in {{formula:12fbc9b0-2206-4d9d-84ef-e8cd3268ebf6}} and {{formula:0d6c8ad6-9141-4d3a-933c-8dd637614b0d}} ; see Figure REF . {{figure:fc09b024-bd4e-41d4-8c35-5b1cf7abde8a}} Figure REF contains a definition of the operators using SQL, as a pragmatic means to provide

In the simplest model of the non-commutative plane (Madore {{cite:33090ec1989a2584574bf08e898a1213e0e4ab35}}) the points {{formula:e6f5be36-6ae9-4093-89f8-049810d5198d}} fulfill {{formula:a4e69edc-edcb-411e-a56e-ca5af77f8dcf}} , preventing as well the singularity creation. Though all these ideas are just free associations (in almost psychoanalytic sense), no better justified is the traditional hypothesis that our space is indeed a continuum of the `exact points'. In fact, if adopting Wigner's observation about the “unreasonable power of mathematics" {{cite:16fc65b78997025ba28cc8d11968a5321bd7f38d}}, the mathematical models, if correct, must appear somewhere in nature. So indeed happens, but with one amendment. The nature might `use' our models in its own way, without caring about the author's intentions. Thus, while the problem of boson-fermion supersymmetry waits to be solved (still no trace of Higgs boson, no gravitinos, etc.), the same mathematical structure appeared in the supersymmetric quantum mechanics (Witten {{cite:b2dd28b7f5d03cecded29d9f360bba2dbda560d8}}, {{cite:36b2fe5e3d4781c1bbca1570eabc2a51ac3a70d4}}) helping to solve exactly a class of spectral problems (Duplij et al {{cite:5aa1964aac43adf9f9a3b51a5acf72442bf2b974}}). While there is still no sign of strings, branes nor extra dimensions, the analogous mathematical structures permit to understand better certain biological phenomena. In fact, the 'clones' of almost all unborn structures start invading the present day physics forming a little-great science in its own right (c.f. “big-bang in probet” etc. {{cite:fb037c5ede0bfce461fa247b520257cba5bb415b}}, {{cite:00220013952ac4f2231533858410c4d4e0adf11a}}). Below, we shall discuss a similar status of the `non-commutative points' which appear in the quantum Hall effect. We shall show that the idea works not only for the static fields but also for time dependent ones, even though the more fundamental hypothesis concerning the granular structure of the space itself is still waiting to be confirmed (or abandoned?). We start from the known facts. The time independent magnetic fields {{formula:81f71bfc-f178-4a88-bee5-9ee060fd991b}} in an open domain of {{formula:17df0544-7a04-420d-ad7c-55612b566b50}} can be described by a class of the vector potentials {{formula:079e896b-00af-4457-9f25-33ea80c0ea2a}} with {{formula:f1a30120-e6e3-4dff-9298-cf040f6fa0bd}} . If {{formula:0aa3c912-bdb2-4264-abe9-28a5be3661ea}} is homogeneous, {{formula:4db77bfb-42d2-4422-89a5-611ded69a4c4}} (for convenience, let {{formula:afc7c765-1acd-44ba-aa4d-b4a879b1649a}} define the {{formula:fd436a82-849d-47cc-9286-8ebf318f8c86}} -axis in {{formula:bcb39e1c-2307-422d-9a14-c7def788a843}} ) then one of natural choices of {{formula:b49aca2b-9b43-4100-8d41-7dfbc2c93924}} is: {{formula:706b88df-c7ec-4a11-a066-1ac24d1b87f9}} interpretable as the vector potential created by a homogeneous current density on the cylindrical surface. The particle motion along the {{formula:0ec93f26-2e58-494f-9e67-02dd2df8dc37}} -direction is then free; hence, we shall be interested only in the motion trajectories on the {{formula:ae8ab0d0-c893-42e7-87f9-3aa4c34817a6}} -plane. In the case of the top 10 ontologies, when the user effort level increases from 1.0 to 2.0, the quality increases from a value between 0.6 and 0.7 to a value between 0.7 and 0.8, again confirming the positive effect of user effort on quality. The top row (REF and REF ) plots the quality of the top 1 ontology, while the bottom row ( REFREF ) plots the quality of the top 10 ontologies, respectively, with user effort level of 1.0 and 2.0. We found significant differences between the top 1 and top 10 cases, in terms of quality. For example, the indegree mechanism results in the highest quality in the top 1 case, but the lowest quality in the top 10 case, which means that the top 1 ontology has a much higher quality than that of the other ontologies in the top 10. That is to say, the use of Indegree causes top ontologies to dominate. This is valuable from the point of view of promoting ontology reuse. When the user effort of annotation is 2.0 (meaning that relatively high effort is required to annotate instances), the quality of the top 1 and top 10 ontologies is as depicted in the figure REF and REF . For the top 1 ontology, Indegree yields the highest average quality, followed by MultiRank, Random and Hits. The quality produced by Indegree, MultiRank, and Random starts between 0.6 and 0.7 (which is the average quality of all the ontologies), and then increases to above 0.9 after 200 iterations, while Hits decrease to below 0.9 (still above 0.8) after around 400 iterations. Here, the Random mechanism seems to do better than Hits, which seems counterintuitive. However, it does make sense that the greater the user effort required for semantic annotation, the less important the ranking mechanism is. As a result it becomes increasingly unlikely that the user will execute the action. Does this mean that less supportive environments actually facilitate ontology reuse? We will see in the following section that this is not the case. The rate of creation of semantic annotations is an important factor for estimating the length of the rest of the simulation. The stop condition of the simulation is a specific number of successfully executed semantic annotation actions, therefore the execution rate of semantic annotation can be used to estimate how long will it take to arrive at this predefined number of actions. The lower the semantic annotation rate, the longer the simulation takes, which corresponds to the reality that if users don't have a high rate of semantic annotation, then the system takes a long time to accumulate a specific amount of annotation information. {{figure:448dd4e7-f6ea-4f98-8abe-8eed3afb6aec}} The REF is the semantic annotation rate when SPL is 1.0, and the REF is the semantic annotation rate when SPL is 2.0. When it cost less (i.e. when SPL is 1.0) to perform semantic annotation, there is no difference between the four mechanisms. When it cost more (i.e. when SPL is 2.0), MultiRank takes the least time, followed by Indegree and Random, and then Hits, which is to say that the if the system uses the MultiRank ranking system, it will take less time to arrive at the predefined number of semantic annotations. In this paper, we have illustrated the use of a simulation to evaluate ranking algorithms and incentive mechanisms in a quantifiable way. Using this technique, different mechanisms can be tested in advance of their deployment in a live social network environment. We have made two assumptions: it is possible to mimic the behavior of a real social network by means of a simulation the simulation model described above is appropriate for modeling information creation in semantic social networks In the past, ranking algorithms have tended to be evaluated only subjectively: if the algorithm produces subjectively accurate results, then it is an appropriate algorithm. The technique presented in this paper provides a measurable alternative. However, the question naturally arises of whether this technique itself is appropriate. How do we evaluate it? Until such time as there are formal techniques for evaluating social network simulations, we must rely on subjective evaluation, choosing the simulation model as sensibly as possible and allowing the results to speak for themselves. We have thoroughly described our simulation model and justified these choices wherever possible: our object model is based on the actor-concept-instance model of social-semantic networks, where change in the network is driven by an iterative process of user actions. Users are guided by metrics of cost, reward in conjunction with predefined metrics of quality as well as the ranking algorithms under investigation. We have presented the results of applying our technique to several common ranking algorithms, and we have shown that these results are reasonable. In future, we intend to test our simulation model against multi-relational ranking algorithms which take advantage of the “semantics” of social-semantic networks. We plan to release our implementation software under an open-source license, so that it can be freely reused by developers of social networking applications. We would like to thank Jim Hendler and Deborah McGuinness for their valuable feedback on various drafts of this paper.

section_text: limitation. Indeed, we have become so used to it that some do not perceive it as a limitation at all. Similar thoughts apply to manuscript formatting. However, the times when paper alone reigned over scholarly communication have certainly passed, and wiki-like platforms provide for simple and efficient means of storing information, updating it and embedding it into a wider context. Cross-field fertilization, for example, is crucial with respect to interdisciplinary research projects, digital libraries and multi-journal (or indeed cross-disciplinary) bibliographic search engines (e.g. Google Scholar), since these dramatically increase the likelihood of, say, a biologist stumbling upon a not primarily biological source relevant to her research (think shape quantification or growth curves, for instance). What options do we have to systematically integrate such cross-disciplinary hidden treasures with the traditional intra-disciplinary background knowledge and with new insights resulting from research? The by now classical example of a wiki environment are the Wikipedias, a set of interlinked wikis in multiple languages where basically anyone can edit any page, regardless of subject matter expertise or command of the respective language. As a consequence of this openness, the larger Wikipedias have a serious problem with vandalism: take an article of your choice and look at its history page for reverts - most of them will be about neutralizing subtle or blunt forms of destructive edits that do nothing to improve the quality of the articles, but may reduce it considerably. Few of these malicious edits persist for long {{cite:af416f344296480bfffcd6f30197db298ecdf485}}, but finding and fixing them takes time that could better be spent on improving articles. This is less of an issue with more popular topics for which large numbers of volunteers may be available to correct "spammy" entries but it is probably fair to assume that most researchers value their time too much to spend it on repeatedly correcting information that had already been correctly entered. Other problems with covering scientific topics at the Wikipedias include the nebulous notability criteria which have to be fulfilled to avoid an article being deleted, and the rejection of "original research" in the sense of not having been peer reviewed before publication. Despite these problems, one scientific journal – RNA Biology – already requires an introductory Wikipedia article for a subset of papers it is to publish {{cite:a30f71133b3fea8a3054e52879bef069f499c2be}}. Peer review is indeed a central aspect of scholarly communication, as it paves the way towards the reproducibility that forms one of the foundations of modern science. Yet we know of no compelling reason to believe that it works better before than after the content concerned has been made public (doing it beforehand was just a practical decision in times when journal space was measured in paper pages), while emerging movements like Open Notebook Science – where claims are linked directly to the underlying data that are being made public as they arise – represent an experiment in this direction whose initial results look promising and call into question Wikipedia's "no original research" as a valid principle for generating encyclopaedic content. Although quite prominent at the moment, the Wikipedias are not the only wikis around, and amongst the more scholarly inclined alternatives, there are even a number of wiki-based journals, though usually with a very narrow scope and/or a low number of articles. On the other hand, Scholarpedia (which has classical peer review and an ISSN and may thus be counted as a wiki journal, too {{cite:000816bf189e5957f9bbb739a991b52db97b05e8}}), OpenWetWare {{cite:c0e435746d21b3dd10eff1c9aa4a07ae6c5a0db6}}, Citizendium {{cite:0ddcd3088812baecd9a1bea3b67b1ea35c377e56}} and the Wikiversities {{cite:70fb4fa9ee1c075ce66062dc257babe3d2dae1bd}} are cross-disciplinary and structured (and of a size, for the moment) such that vandalism and notability are not really a problem. With minor exceptions, real names are required at the first three, and anybody can contribute to entries about anything, particularly in their fields of expertise. None of these is even close to providing the vast amount of context existing in the English Wikipedia but the difference is much less dramatic if the latter were broken down to scholarly useful content. Out of these four wikis, only OpenWetWare is explicitly designed to harbour original research, while the others allow different amounts thereof. Furthermore, a growing number of yet more specialized scholarly wikis exist (e.g. WikiGenes {{cite:1e68054761a4b30178f369318e1baed9da0a055c}}, the Encyclopedia of Earth {{cite:a9df479b2a9ab7dbfb5dcae64233df9ad8095b28}}, the Encyclopedia of Cosmos {{cite:113c323ace8576d5c9f71cbb01d6573af07d9df3}}, the Dispersive PDE Wiki {{cite:b32a7f53be14016a8fff9427eb4d6dd6b4d84b43}}, or the Polymath Wiki {{cite:4dc982d804e6dff32c611a69ffe0caaced7e28a8}}), which can teach us about the usefulness of wikis within specific academic fields. Despite the above-mentioned tensions between public participation and expertise in the collaborative structuring of knowledge, it is not unreasonable to expect that these can be overcome by suitably designed public knowledge environments, much like Citizen Science projects involve the public in the generation of scientific data. One approach at such a design is represented by Citizendium. The founder of Citizendium – Larry Sanger – is the co-founder of Wikipedia. The two projects share the common goal of providing free knowledge to the public, they are based on variants of the same software platform, and they use the same Creative Commons-Attribution-Share Alike license {{cite:a3c7099c5cbbbb9286420a191e45b1d185caf010}}. Yet they differ in a number of important ways, such that Citizendium can be seen as composed of a Wikipedia core (stripped down in terms of content, templates, categories and policies), with elements added that are characteristic of the other wiki environments introduced above: A review process leading to stable versions (as at Scholarpedia), an open education environment (as at Wikiversity) and an open research environment (as at OpenWetWare). The gossip-based distributed protocol algorithms obtained in {{cite:ab680613a2a9b53682a4121d6646288be9863c73}} for complex problems for a set of nodes in Euclidean space are implemented by constructing an approximated minimum spanning tree. With the increasing importance and presence of sensor as well as P2P networks, networks have a high level of congestion and because of that the theory concerning information survivability becomes very important. One source of inspiration for mathematical modeling problems of information survivability in this kind of networks is the epidemiology. The epidemiology community has developed several stochastic models for studying the spread and die-out of diseases in a population. The two most relevant ones are the SIR and SIS models. Both are stochastic models of the spread of disease through a population, where the susceptible nodes can get infected on contact with infected neighbors. The infected hosts eventually die (in the SIR model) or recover and become susceptible again (in the SIS model). The point of view adopted in {{cite:c18a657151d844e2317354475a031b4c41475f1b}} was the SIS model. Under this model a node is susceptible to a data item when it is online and under normal operation. When the nodes start to fail, they become immune during their failure, and later they become susceptible again when they are back online. Some results obtained in {{cite:c18a657151d844e2317354475a031b4c41475f1b}} are very useful to analyze the survival of a infection in a population, based on the graph theory results similar to the ones mentioned in {{cite:1d257b7dbd576162e50b0fd2e2522641206bffb6}}, {{cite:b58ff379c9a9fc4155002c5989753d51510f6573}}, {{cite:b4bb1fc5fc246b2f37635eca0e9424f0733e2f70}}. In computer security one of the important issues that have been studied under SIS and SIR infection spreading mathematical models are the virus propagation as well as worms on Internet, from where, the exponential spread of them and the epidemic thresholds can be estimated {{cite:062ae13604be0f10ef5e29b241400b5635e9cfae}},{{cite:a27241d2e72a4a583c93d4e51ebd75cfe0eab424}}, {{cite:e08e0f101176fc271b230162a1baffe0cf2d97e8}}. Let us suppose that we have a sensor/P2P/social network of {{formula:01eacaba-879f-40ed-8939-b44cb0a4b00f}} nodes (sensors or computers or people) and {{formula:24c8b50d-80ca-4493-970e-08564f08e5c4}} directed links between them. Let us also assume that we take very small discrete timesteps of size {{formula:e93b9cb6-3ead-4c9a-a46e-4bb0a5111fad}} where {{formula:20aee331-4942-43df-8bbe-2480527ade0a}} . The survivability results in {{cite:c18a657151d844e2317354475a031b4c41475f1b}} apply equally well to continuous systems. Within a {{formula:bbac610e-feb5-4fc2-aa35-4d2d8c9fa937}} time interval, each node {{formula:99615023-8ce1-43a8-a75c-39a3d76d8058}} has probabiity {{formula:810065fa-b8f1-4d51-9539-7ddff35a0799}} of trying to broadcast its information every time step, and each link {{formula:f818d4ed-66f0-4f62-b8db-d9194baf2a1a}} has a probability {{formula:2d365270-e055-4aa8-a590-74559eea4962}} of being up, and thus correctly propagating the information to node {{formula:39735cd6-8582-4ddb-b9d0-b68d30ee988e}} . Each node {{formula:d5cdf15d-0278-4736-a063-595928dea8cd}} also has a node failure probability {{formula:ef9cfc4f-ad16-44d0-997f-836d69f922e4}} (e.g., due to battery failure in sensors). Every dead node {{formula:104bea9d-6d00-49c8-b9d8-bb0e8703bcb5}} has a rate {{formula:74c28324-ce4c-4dee-9ddd-dcf1ebcbc8dd}} of returning to the up state, but without any information in its memory (e.g., due to the periodic replacement of dead batteries).
