section_text: limitations. We conclude by summarizing our contributions and suggesting future work in Sec. . In this section we present a framework for the evaluation of query segmentation algorithms based on IR performance. Let {{formula:6d94cdd4-e27d-4dae-8e5f-cfb1748db632}} denote a search query and let {{formula:f2aa0856-8ee7-452d-862b-dd05c95b6640}} denote a segmentation of {{formula:135141e8-de7e-45b8-864a-05adafb2f560}} such that a simple concatenation of the {{formula:8734c99b-c036-41bb-ab02-bee5642088b0}} segments equals {{formula:08b8dffa-878a-4eea-8c3a-c1642d3a1dba}} , i.e., we have {{formula:85efa2dc-14df-4d08-8046-3bc9c1496369}} , where + represents the concatenation operator. We are given a segmentation algorithm {{formula:9f5eddad-4abb-458a-907b-af6d77af6cac}} and the task is to evaluate its performance. We require the following resources: A test set {{formula:c3e24b11-bb9d-46c6-b5ee-344645aeff2e}} of unquoted search queries. A set {{formula:4f7b0479-24c3-42cf-b561-78913fac685d}} of documents (or URLs) out of which search results will be retrieved. Relevance judgments {{formula:eefb08c2-8257-4e9c-9427-b4ebe8e261e9}} for query-URL pairs {{formula:bdac219d-0b41-4944-93f1-01a6d93042be}} . The set of all relevance judgments are collectively denoted by {{formula:1a50494d-f3e6-4ed2-a267-3a1228f64b61}} . An IR engine that supports quoted queries as input. The resources needed by our evaluation framework are essentially the same as those needed for the training and testing of a standard IR engine, namely, queries, a document corpus and set of relevance judgments. Akin to the training examples required for an IR engine, we only require relevance judgments for a small and appropriate subset of {{formula:1cfbe40e-31fa-4935-8538-ae9c2b25b686}} (each query needs only the documents in its own pool to be judged) {{cite:7fff56e86ec546543919f78bbe94009e30b96930}}. It is useful to separate the evaluation of segmentation performance, from the question of how to best exploit the segments to retrieve the most relevant documents. From an IR perspective, a natural interpretation of a segment could be that it consists of words that must appear together, in the same order, in documents where the segment is deemed to match {{cite:c8efd40c87072e4f8b2dce8189fbee7bb82be08a}}. This can be referred to as ordered contiguity matching. While this can be easily enforced in modern IR engines through use of double quotes around segments, we observe that not all segments must be used this way (see {{cite:2a275e9db6e3ec5bae088a40123293a7167fec17}} for related ideas and experiments in a different context). Some segments may admit more general matching criteria, such as unordered or intruded contiguity (e.g., a segment a b may be allowed to match b a or a c b in the document). The case of unordered intruded matching may be restricted under linguistic dependence assumptions (e.g., a b can match a of b or b in a). Finally, some segments may even play non-matching roles (e.g., when the segment specifies user intent, like how to and where is). Thus, there may be several different ways to exploit the segments discovered by a segmentation algorithm. Even within the same query, different segments may need to be treated differently. For instance, in the query cannot view | word files | windows 7, the first one might be matched using intruded ordered occurrence (cannot properly view), the second segment may be matched under a linguistic dependency model (files in word) and the last one under ordered contiguity. Intruded contiguity and linguistic dependency may be difficult to implement for the broad class of general Web search queries. Identifying how the various segments of a query should be ideally matched in the document is quite a challenging and unsolved research problem. On the other hand, an exhaustive expansion scheme, where every segment is expanded in every possible way, is computationally expensive and might introduce noise. Moreover, current commercial IR engines do not support any syntax to specify linguistic dependence or intruded or unordered occurrence based matching. Hence, in order to keep the evaluation framework in line with the current IR systems, we focus on ordered contiguity matching which is easily implemented through the use of double quotes around segments. However, we note that the philosophy of the framework does not change with increased sophistication in the retrieval system – only the expansion sets for the queries have to be appropriately modified. {{table:b400a932-5466-41a2-8323-83a25cb6bf04}} We propose an evaluation framework for segmentation algorithms that generates all possible quoted versions of a segmented query (see Table REF ) and submits each quoted version to the IR engine. The corresponding ranked lists of retrieved documents are then assessed against relevance judgments available for the query-URL pairs. The IR quality of the best-performing quoted version is used to measure performance of the segmentation algorithm. We now formally specify our evaluation framework that computes what we call a Quoted Version Retrieval Score (QVRS) for the segmentation algorithm given the test set {{formula:5d77be9f-27b3-4bda-a03d-a58b4fde6600}} of queries, the document pool {{formula:b7cc0298-c62d-473f-adaa-c68fa9a28a7a}} and the relevance judgments {{formula:c5bd25ae-b0e0-4812-b94a-e9cef1a17c4e}} for query-URL pairs. Let the segmentation output by algorithm {{formula:3afca62e-64bb-44bf-a46e-921424c9ea68}} be denoted by {{formula:b05ad718-34af-467b-b944-e55e38c4318c}} . We generate all possible quoted versions of the query {{formula:b7522c72-707d-41b7-9ae5-1b493e8eb5b5}} based on the segments in {{formula:c6b728d5-cd21-4f45-82c3-9a41996955b7}} . In particular, we define {{formula:3cf1ec0a-8f64-45e7-b736-4219248fdea6}} with no quotes on any of the segments, {{formula:9a3981d5-9479-43c5-a9cc-7d24dbaa55b9}} with quotes only around the last segment {{formula:48dd3a22-6dc7-4e68-9839-746d91a916d3}} , and so on. Since there are {{formula:fed22286-3d80-449c-8e3b-e62d090f54df}} segments in {{formula:bdd46c0b-67b7-4e1e-83e8-7f1db284fc1a}} , this process will generate {{formula:4b20b739-58a9-42b3-8fd6-e5b15e22d12a}} versions of the query, {{formula:ead69fc3-ce7c-4a92-8824-c19a9536569f}} , {{formula:145139c3-a161-42c9-b2ed-82285add4243}} . For example, the query versions "harry potter" "game" and "harry potter" game are equivalent in terms of the input semantics of an IR engine. section_text: limitations: None of the existing algorithms improves over FFT's runtime for the whole range of sparse signals, i.e., {{formula:1aa8aa7e-fcb2-4723-8d60-77866fd3e987}} . Most of the aforementioned algorithms are quite complex, and suffer from large “big-Oh” constants (the algorithm of {{cite:a46529e50cc6cfd67e34378afda81b3bc83aded9}} is an exception, but has a running time that is polynomial in {{formula:bf607d59-32ae-41cc-8868-603a5a3b609f}} ). In this paper, we address these limitations by presenting two new algorithms for the sparse Fourier transform. We require that the length {{formula:8b045610-00f8-4b7f-947a-9406a07f9b58}} of the input signal is a power of 2. We show: An {{formula:b8ad5bac-3b07-4410-893e-af07841a9026}} -time algorithm for the exactly {{formula:c370491f-b2e9-41e2-a972-652389c52c1a}} -sparse case, and An {{formula:4c477e70-38dd-4586-8522-cb6915dc0c93}} -time algorithm for the general case. The key property of both algorithms is their ability to achieve {{formula:3899dcd9-a55f-48f0-9a55-954982fb4bda}} time, and thus improve over the FFT, for any {{formula:62ff7f2d-71db-4b5f-9628-8473b9022830}} . These algorithms are the first known algorithms that satisfy this property. Moreover, if one assume that FFT is optimal and hence the DFT cannot be computed in less than {{formula:6b7c2cc7-c138-4dc1-98b6-3d09b5412370}} time, the algorithm for the exactly {{formula:5ecf689a-44f2-4879-b3c4-8596f3471950}} -sparse case is optimalOne also needs to assume that {{formula:aa61c0b0-5501-4c23-8f31-37d39dd12322}} divides {{formula:65ac4118-a9e6-406b-95a1-c6ee2df15782}} . See Section for more details. as long as {{formula:84eb86bd-3fd5-4c1f-9ed2-5ceaa36d3b2b}} . Under the same assumption, the result for the general case is at most one {{formula:62cc1679-f9a0-4338-b9b9-ff84ea4a996d}} factor away from the optimal runtime for the case of “large” sparsity {{formula:2d02f7f8-d63d-4207-8951-5df2c5446f85}} . Furthermore, our algorithm for the exactly sparse case (depicted as Algorithm on page 5) is quite simple and has low big-Oh constants. In particular, our preliminary implementation of a variant of this algorithm is faster than FFTW, a highly efficient implementation of the FFT, for {{formula:c51fccae-f8bc-4c6a-b17a-60ebb17a92c3}} and {{formula:c21a1b25-1602-4e5d-b6dc-c60a193264b8}} {{cite:48e0995af4674ef14bd906118faf16623062018f}}. In contrast, for the same signal size, prior algorithms were faster than FFTW only for {{formula:b0df3822-4abf-4594-ac2e-810c46e07472}} {{cite:a46529e50cc6cfd67e34378afda81b3bc83aded9}}.Note that both numbers ({{formula:e698c8e0-cd66-4668-ad65-8f20093bb48a}} and {{formula:43c96c8b-9182-4aae-aabf-0959b70224e2}} ) are for the exactly k-sparse case. The algorithm in {{cite:a46529e50cc6cfd67e34378afda81b3bc83aded9}} can deal with the general case, but the empirical runtimes are higher. We complement our algorithmic results by showing that any algorithm that works for the general case must use at least {{formula:3814528d-1e25-49ab-8dd0-3870a2f46b7a}} samples from {{formula:acdd9996-b16e-4100-89aa-b17a077ea4ff}} . The lower bound uses techniques from {{cite:b8d2d7750d09bfa52007969ef0923ae18b991849}}, which shows a lower bound of {{formula:efc39daf-1978-463b-b478-ca1a2011918f}} for the number of arbitrary linear measurements needed to compute the {{formula:8baf2b77-e288-449e-bfd2-21c5d35a77c5}} -sparse approximation of an {{formula:02c8dea7-fdb5-407c-b11f-17a8b356e19e}} -dimensional vector {{formula:55490e1e-367f-45f0-9db4-56f10c78e523}} . In comparison to {{cite:b8d2d7750d09bfa52007969ef0923ae18b991849}}, our bound is slightly worse but it holds even for adaptive sampling, where the algorithm selects the samples based on the values of the previously sampled coordinates.Note that if we allow arbitrary adaptive linear measurements of a vector {{formula:999707b0-cb43-4087-b934-b65c2a1208ad}} , then its {{formula:99171cae-5529-44aa-9af3-689d5f65cbcd}} -sparse approximation can be computed using only {{formula:c33cf0f1-da21-4505-85cb-7eadd8415370}} samples {{cite:09f35e0d1da5a7c44d542656e248770b8c7f38e6}}. Therefore, our lower bound holds only where the measurements, although adaptive, are limited to those induced by the Fourier matrix. This is the case when we want to compute a sparse approximation to {{formula:8ba0e0dc-1828-430a-bba8-a57d7e4114cb}} from samples of {{formula:ee7fd03e-bd7a-411a-b775-0956ab988b01}} . Note that our algorithms are non-adaptive, and thus limited by the more stringent lower bound of {{cite:b8d2d7750d09bfa52007969ef0923ae18b991849}}. We start with an overview of the techniques used in prior works. At a high level, sparse Fourier algorithms work by binning the Fourier coefficients into a small number of bins. Since the signal is sparse in the frequency domain, each bin is likelyOne can randomize the positions of the frequencies by sampling the signal in time domain appropriately {{cite:5a107eeb4ba3d2f710c05b17ee8a0a2382e457d7}}, {{cite:96e6c90cafca4fb91bb5de2d02c7734e0cbdd923}}. See Preliminaries for the description. to have only one large coefficient, which can then be located (to find its position) and estimated (to find its value). The binning has to be done in sublinear time, and thus these algorithms bin the Fourier coefficients using an {{formula:0fef6199-0687-4e18-84a6-740bd598a44d}} -dimensional filter vector {{formula:e15322c8-1d12-489d-8f0f-21170ee0d19a}} that is concentrated both in time and frequency. That is, {{formula:dde79899-ec52-4992-b1e0-97cef5193c5b}} is zero except at a small number of time coordinates, and its Fourier transform {{formula:e9a9b1c0-5711-4f63-ba82-516a3e10157a}} is negligible except at a small fraction (about {{formula:33005aaa-555e-4d85-bf73-3906e4a0dfe1}} ) of the frequency coordinates, representing the filter's “pass” region. Each bin essentially receives only the frequencies in a narrow range corresponding to the pass region of the (shifted) filter {{formula:cd615049-f9e8-4f4c-9bd4-eab3d34796ab}} , and the pass regions corresponding to different bins are disjoint. In this paper, we use filters introduced in {{cite:a46529e50cc6cfd67e34378afda81b3bc83aded9}}. Those filters (defined in more detail in Preliminaries) have the property that the value of {{formula:7e5e0f47-f162-4136-bff0-5cf091d969ff}} is “large” over a constant fraction of the pass region, referred to as the “super-pass” region. We say that a coefficient is “isolated” if it falls into a filter's super-pass region and no other coefficient falls into filter's pass region. Since the super-pass region of our filters is a constant fraction of the pass region, the probability of isolating a coefficient is constant. To achieve the stated running times, we need a fast method for locating and estimating isolated coefficients. Further, our algorithm is iterative, so we also need a fast method for updating the signal so that identified coefficients are not considered in future iterations. Below, we describe these methods in more detail. Our location and estimation methods depends on whether we handle the exactly sparse case or the general case. In the exactly sparse case, we show how to estimate the position of an isolated Fourier coefficient using only two samples of the filtered signal. Specifically, we show that the phase difference between the two samples is linear in the index of the coefficient, and hence we can recover the index by estimating the phases. This approach is inspired by the frequency offset estimation in orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM),

section_text: verbs that were most common in the one-verb sentences were “saj al", “qAl", “>aEolan", “$Arik", “kAn", “daEA", “fAz", “balag", “>aHoraz", and “lotaqiy". These are glossed by Google Translate as: record, said, announced, was, called, beat, was, made, and assess, definitely a different sort of verb than the ones we see commonly in the in the text generally. Even among the verbs that happen commonly in both the text in general and the one-verb sentences, we observe different usages. The most common verb in general, “kAn" (was), occurs with another verb phrase as an argument about 400 times in the treebank. The second-most common verb in general and in the one-verb sentences, “qAl" (“declared/said"), most often occurs with an SBAR (indicating a nested clause) in general, but of course these usages do not occur in the one-verb sentences. In experiments with the nearly-unannotatedvery lightly marked-up with SGML text distributed with the treebank, we made use of AraMorph {{cite:b7421dddd88f2bfe5e7824f4918d720a58031b52}}, a Free Software version of the Buckwalter morphological analyzer that handles Unicode text. The goal with the unannotated text was to see which subcategory frames we could observe in sentences with a single verb – the rich Arabic morphology usually marks case on nouns, which should allow us to find many arguments to verbs. We could then compare the valencies learned from the unannotated corpus with those that are more easily observable from the treebank. If the valencies that we discover with the unannotated approach are close to those learned from the treebank, and we get a broad coverage over the verbs observed in the corpus, then this would provide an argument that the technique works fairly well for Arabic, and we could continue using it as we acquire more textual data for more under-resourced languages. However, Buckwalter-style morphological analyzers do not account for morphological ambiguity, which would present difficulties in the long run. This problem is particularly dire because the Arabic script is an abjad, which is to say that it only records the consonants for each word. There is an optional system for annotating the vowel sounds as well, but it is often not used in practice. This presents a problem for Arabic-language NLP systems, though, since a word without context rarely has a unique morphological analysis. In fact, within the corpus, we observed a mean of about 7.5 possible Buckwalter analyses per word, with {{formula:f97e16c4-3801-4518-ac10-46f90adfab6d}} , and a maximum of 86. The word with 86 Buckwalter analyses can mean, at least, “one", “and scrutinize", “and sharpen", or “and be furious". We also briefly experimented with a Quechua morphological analyzer, Michael Gasser's AntiMorfo system gasser:antimorfo; it can analyze Quechua verbs, nouns, and adjectives. We also see morphological ambiguity in Quechua words, although it is not nearly so striking, largely due to the orthography with vowels. We saw a mean of 1.7 analyses per word, with {{formula:76b7792e-334c-4282-8a79-be1c6c62a40f}} , and a maximum of 10. For Quechua, we used a small corpus produced by the AVENUE project, described in {{cite:f1aee043616d4089ade1290b736ca3b747c67e9e}}, which includes bitext elicited from native speakers, and monolingual text, both from UN documents and local stories. Interestingly, with the FST-based morphological analysis, we cannot tell whether a word is definitely a verb. For example, waqaychu may be a verb, noun, or infinitive, as “waqa" is in AntiMorfo's lexicon as a verb root, and “waqay" as a noun root. So to get good results for Quechua, we would need a POS tagger or other means to choose between analyses. As far as treebanks of Quechua, for evaluating an automatically-extracted Quechua verb lexicon, to our knowledge there is no large one available, although Rios et al. are developing a small one rios. While the problem of discovering grammatical subcategories of verbs remains interesting, and solutions to that problem would be of practical use, it is almost definitely not enough to use only a morphological analyzer and a medium-sized unannotated corpus for this purpose; disregarding sentences with more than one verb leads to misleading view of the language as a whole, and selection preferences learned from these sentences would not be suitable for parsing most sentences. To make better use of the existing data, it would be helpful to have a chunker to find the boundaries of clauses and noun phrases, as in {{cite:84562dd6e84c24baa16efff0bed45f94624901ed}}. For Czech verbs, Bojar similarly used finite-state rules to find coordinated and subordinate clauses bojar:2003. While ambiguity in morphological analysis can be a hurdle in any language, the vowel-free nature of typical Arabic text presents a particularly serious one; we would like to be able to use any available unannotated text, but without morphological disambiguation, we are left with many possible interpretations for most tokens. This could be mitigated with software like MADA+TOKAN habash:2009, which chooses the most likely morphological analysis for a given context; for other languages, such as Quechua, similar tools will need to be developed. Even with proper POS tagging, morphological disambiguation, and chunking, we are still faced with the problem of negative evidence; without a very large corpus, we cannot say with confidence that a given verb cannot appear with certain arguments, simply because it has not yet been observed with those arguments. This difficulty suggests an active learning approach, perhaps coupled with crowdsourcing. We could imagine a system that generates sentences to test the hypothesis that a given verb may be used with a given subcategorization frame, then presents those sentences to human users for grammaticality judgments.

section_text: future work, including tying in to Homotopy Type Theory (in the sense of {{cite:0dac6ba5791631780ab426c0a70bba405bd70f8b}} and {{cite:847e79ffe6d3ad0200d6ef07f208fa20819e96d4}}) and other projects. We use the notation {{formula:9ba977e7-6be4-4cdb-b33f-8a484e13716b}} to denote a set with one element. Given any category {{formula:1bc0ce51-7a52-4133-b917-34da79847a4c}} , we denote the category of all functors {{formula:899f5e7d-582c-439c-9327-c96db539c19e}} by {{formula:fcf06dff-fc4d-4407-bc9c-ea045cdc9ebc}} . The terminal object in {{formula:6b70d36c-520b-4fb2-aed1-8749456b3bd1}} sends each object in {{formula:361332ad-c0ab-4c9c-9f41-5ada7e8545cb}} to {{formula:e5c8848a-3c5f-4ac1-bab7-82edcee2a3eb}} ; we denote it by {{formula:048d2fb2-299c-449c-b7d1-68769648b49e}} . We use {{formula:e85858a6-5256-4860-8794-8d614b134aa2}} to denote a discrete category with one object. For any category {{formula:cb9d390b-d5d4-4500-9552-3a63d204674f}} , there is a one-to-one correspondence between the objects in {{formula:ec3b0c34-4be3-4c2c-893a-dd46cde31746}} and the functors {{formula:0da52aea-5388-4429-8b5a-81737ba9dd77}} . Thus we may denote an object {{formula:af1e10a3-4f22-4f8a-af03-f9a3c42912fe}} by a functor {{formula:a8bd7994-6745-4c3e-9cf9-5aba6da8dfa5}} . In particular, we elide the difference between a set and a functor {{formula:f1852e05-7b55-47f2-a4f1-af3f6fbb2bba}} . We draw schemas in one of two ways. When trying to save space, we draw our objects as concisely-labeled nodes and our morphisms as concisely-labeled arrows; when trying to be more expressive, we draw our objects as text boxes and put as much text in them (and on each arrow) as is necessary to be clear (see {{cite:786a7e889483b9dc754641133ea5f1fab96d72f5}}). For example, we might draw the indexing category for directed graphs in either of the following two ways: {{formula:b35830be-5be7-4a34-b7b6-fb8f3e01b3b7}} When in the typographical context of inline text we are discussing an object that has been elsewhere displayed as a textbox (such as an edge), we may represent it with corner symbols (e.g. as {{formula:b659f44d-acca-40bd-b5e0-dd08f8cad13d}} an edge{{formula:e8e36bed-69d4-4d2b-b168-c84d0a014fdb}} ) to avoid various spacing issues that can arise. Given two categories, there are generally many functors from one to the other; however, if the objects and arrows are labeled coherently, there are many fewer functors that roughly respect the labelings. We will usually be explicit when defining functors, but we will also take care that our functors respect labeling to the extent possible. I would like to thank Henrik Forssell, Peter Gates, Rich Haney, Eric Prud'hommeaux, and Emily Riehl for many useful discussions. The basic mantra is that a database schema is a small category {{formula:aea49ad8-3f32-4d23-aea5-c97d39830396}} and an instance is a functor {{formula:9621a244-df3e-4296-a2ac-3d39b442ba7f}} , where {{formula:5ba5f5fc-25bc-4e78-b84c-220c0f07e2ee}} is the category of sets.If one prefers, {{formula:a32f377f-927c-4fb7-b81b-a05e9650cb54}} can be replaced by the category of finite sets or by the category Types for some {{formula:f6809178-478e-49bd-b16d-41b43ef01e34}} -calculus. To recall these ideas, we take liberally from {{cite:46bb68c307a45c3dbb22a4518bf779e6dab6e590}}, though more details and clarification are given there. Readers who are familiar with the basic setup and data migration functors can skip to Section REF . In {{cite:46bb68c307a45c3dbb22a4518bf779e6dab6e590}} a category {{formula:80834321-9c4e-4fe1-8b5b-2b47b936e156}} of categorical schemas and translations is defined and an equivalence of categories {{formula:e3125982-5b10-454f-aaef-3db7925fefa8}} is proved, where {{formula:b8a28364-0416-4ae7-8990-c8ae78d32b0a}} is the category of small categories. The difference between {{formula:354811df-30b0-44b2-bdf2-da33f5729b15}} and {{formula:5c4e993e-916e-45c3-b239-f0326e42da35}} is that an object of the former is a chosen presentation of a category, by generators and relations. Given the equivalence (REF ), we can and do elide the difference between schemas and small categories. Roughly, a schema {{formula:43a51b45-f7ca-42c5-bfc7-235198c9d33a}} consists of a graph {{formula:dc9e6ff1-5499-42d9-b46b-9c8d5ecf1aff}} together with an equivalence relation on the set of paths of {{formula:5726bce8-b8fc-45cb-9484-85d1d6f4b5ef}} . Each object {{formula:01a96570-4b10-4d25-91ad-b9f085d85b33}} represents a table (or more precisely the ID column of a table), and each arrow {{formula:efc219aa-e787-4203-b1ea-4f58770e2d55}} emanating from {{formula:c4c4fc62-e5cd-4ff3-9b7e-99612d35bbb8}} represents a column of table {{formula:02590aa5-80b7-4e0f-b7e5-2999ed5f0ab8}} , taking values in the ID column of table {{formula:ce146be5-84dd-4cee-99f2-a4d3e459fd22}} . An example should clarify the ideas. Example 2.1.1 As a typical database example, consider the bookkeeping necessary to run a department store. We keep track of a set of employees and a set of departments. For each employee {{formula:4aedbd0c-db25-4dcb-b5d5-fcafe3fa9acf}} , we keep track of the first name of {{formula:5ebb4a8a-003d-4c2a-9add-1547d1056373}} , which is a FirstNameString, the last name of {{formula:83687a76-6937-4643-bb24-61e4bfd88539}} , which is a LastNameString, the manager of {{formula:29c99b32-277d-4fbc-8b45-20f2e9bfea3e}} , which is an Employee, and the department that {{formula:8c0ad384-3a14-4568-9c2f-cdeb270232c8}} works in, which is a Department. For each department {{formula:9e643424-de82-440c-8c94-b466df0bd644}} , we keep track of the name of {{formula:e0b4814a-3693-48c1-bfbc-a48b7f15aecf}} , which is a DepartmentNameString, and the secretary of {{formula:598caae3-1f40-4499-89fa-e446c9e6c37a}} , which is an Employee. Suppose further that we make the following two rules. For every employee {{formula:ced29128-e86d-4cbc-9ad9-310a7b24e3a0}} , the manager of {{formula:ea134d24-a8b5-4fc1-956f-2fe3c9b0e32b}} works in the same department that {{formula:4338bce8-c007-49fe-a990-29fed4cbf05c}} works in. For every department {{formula:1dce9b1c-29ef-4ed1-b02d-72bd2eec22dc}} , the secretary of {{formula:14f7e9b9-25f3-49bf-82b5-4b785a650bd8}} works in department {{formula:9952e009-9897-41e1-b14b-34316d6c13fd}} . This is all captured neatly, with nothing left out and nothing else added, by the category presented below: {{formula:f5fd1ffc-44bc-4e27-a00b-241994563928}} The underlined statements at the top indicate pairs of commutative (i.e. equivalent) paths; each path is indicated by its source object followed by the sequence of arrows that composes it. The objects, arrows, and equivalences in {{formula:7705ecfa-cbab-4719-aff3-8763ae711b3f}} correspond to the tables, columns, and rules laid out at the beginning of this example. The collection of data on a schema is typically presented in table form. Display (REF ) shows how a database with schema {{formula:43a5f81c-e0e5-4755-8406-7af8647021c7}} might look at a particular moment in time. {{formula:702d18a0-d918-4ce0-80a0-cf2b65506ace}} {{formula:bde813fc-2cfc-47ea-883c-92ec92747d9a}} Every table has an ID column, and in every table each cell references a cell in the ID column of some table. For example, cells in the secretary column of the Department table refer to cells in the ID column of the Employee table. Finally, one checks that Rule 1 and Rule 2 hold. For example, let {{formula:0b2cb04d-d7ad-4c4d-8734-b782755240a0}} be Employee 101. He works in Department q10 and his manager is Employee 103. Employee 103 works in Department q10 as well, as required. The point is that the data in (REF ) conform precisely to the schema {{formula:429de942-b968-470b-865e-10138cef5c3c}} from Diagram (REF ).
